chapters.title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: A green and yellow parrot hanging in a cage outside the door kept repeating over and over:
“Allez vous-en! Allez vous-en! Sapristi! That’s all right!”

He could speak a little Spanish, and also a language that nobody understood — unless it was the mockingbird on the other side of the door, who whistled his fluty notes out on the breeze with maddening persistence.
Mr. Pontellier, unable to read his newspaper with any comfort, rose with a look and a word of disgust.

He walked down the gallery and across the narrow footbridges connecting the Lebrun cottages to one another. He had been sitting by the door of the main house. The parrot and the mockingbird belonged to Madame Lebrun, and they had every right to make whatever noise they pleased. Mr. Pontellier had the privilege of removing himself from their company when they stopped being entertaining.

He stopped at the door of his own cottage — the fourth from the main building and second to last. He settled into a wicker rocker on the porch and tried again to read the paper. It was Sunday; the paper was a day old. The Sunday editions hadn’t yet reached Grand Isle. He already knew the market reports by heart, and he skimmed restlessly over the editorials and news he hadn’t had time to read before leaving New Orleans the day before.
Mr. Pontellier wore glasses. He was forty, medium height, slender, with a slight stoop. His hair was brown and straight, parted on one side. His beard was neatly trimmed.

Every so often he looked up from the paper and glanced around. The noise from the main house was louder than ever. The Farival twins were playing a piano duet from Zampa. Madame Lebrun was bustling in and out, calling instructions in a high voice to a yard boy whenever she was inside, and directions in the same high voice to a dining-room servant whenever she came out. She was a bright, pretty woman who always wore white, with short sleeves, her stiff skirts rustling as she moved. Farther along, in front of one of the cottages, a woman in black walked back and forth at a slow, deliberate pace, counting her beads. Many of the pension’s guests had gone across to the Chêniere Caminada in Beaudelet’s boat to hear mass. Some young people were out under the water oaks playing croquet. Mr. Pontellier’s two children were among them — sturdy little boys of four and five. A quadroon nurse followed them at a distance with a distant, dreamy air.

Mr. Pontellier lit a cigar and smoked, letting the newspaper drift from his hand. He fixed his gaze on a white sunshade advancing at a snail’s pace from the beach. Between the gaunt trunks of the water oaks and across the stretch of yellow chamomile he could see it clearly. The gulf looked far away, melting hazily into the blue horizon. The sunshade continued to approach. Beneath its pink-lined shelter were his wife, Mrs. Pontellier, and young Robert Lebrun. When they reached the cottage, the two sat down on the upper porch step facing each other, each leaning against a post, with every appearance of having tired themselves out.
“What folly! Bathing at such an hour in such heat!” exclaimed Mr. Pontellier. He himself had gone in at daylight — which was why the morning had seemed so long to him.

“You’re burnt beyond recognition,” he added, looking at his wife as one looks at a piece of valuable personal property that has suffered some damage. She held up her hands — strong, shapely hands — and surveyed them critically, pulling her fawn-colored sleeves above the wrists. Looking at her hands reminded her of her rings, which she had given her husband to hold before going into the water. She silently held out her hand to him, and he, understanding, took the rings from his vest pocket and dropped them into her open palm. She slipped them on; then, clasping her knees, she looked over at Robert and began to laugh. The rings sparkled on her fingers. He smiled back.

“What is it?” asked Pontellier, watching them with lazy amusement. It was some bit of nonsense, some adventure out in the water, and they both tried to tell it at once. The story seemed far less funny in the telling. They all felt this — and so did Mr. Pontellier. He yawned and stretched. Then he got up, saying he had half a mind to walk over to Klein’s hotel and play a game of billiards.
“Come along, Lebrun,” he offered. But Robert said quite frankly that he preferred to stay where he was and talk to Mrs. Pontellier.
“Well, send him on his way when he bores you, Edna,” her husband said as he prepared to leave.
“Here, take the umbrella,” she called, holding it out to him. He took the sunshade, lifted it over his head, came down the steps, and walked away.

“Coming back for dinner?” his wife called after him. He paused a moment and shrugged. He felt his vest pocket — there was a ten-dollar bill there. He didn’t know; perhaps he’d be back for the early dinner, perhaps not. It depended on the company at Klein’s and the size of the game. He didn’t say any of this, but she understood, and laughed, nodding goodbye.
Both boys wanted to follow their father when they saw him leaving. He kissed them and promised to bring back bonbons and peanuts.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: Mrs. Pontellier’s eyes were quick and bright, a yellowish brown close to the color of her hair. She had a way of turning them swiftly on something and holding them there, as if lost in some inner maze of thought.

Her eyebrows were a shade darker than her hair — thick, nearly horizontal, underscoring the depth of her eyes. She was handsome rather than beautiful. Her face was captivating for its frankness of expression and a subtle, contradictory play of features. Her manner drew people in.
Robert rolled a cigarette. He smoked cigarettes because he couldn’t afford cigars, he said. He had a cigar in his pocket that Mr. Pontellier had given him, and was saving it for after dinner.

This seemed entirely natural. In coloring he wasn’t unlike his companion. His clean-shaved face made the resemblance more apparent than it might otherwise have been. No shadow of worry crossed his open face. His eyes gathered in and reflected the light and ease of the summer day.

Mrs. Pontellier reached for a palm-leaf fan lying on the porch and began to fan herself, while Robert drew light puffs from his cigarette. They talked without stopping — about everything around them; about their adventure in the water, which had grown amusing again in the retelling; about the wind, the trees, the people who had gone to the Chêniere; about the children playing croquet under the oaks, and the Farival twins, who were now working through the overture to The Poet and the Peasant.

Robert talked quite a lot about himself. He was very young and didn’t know any better. Mrs. Pontellier talked a little about herself for the same reason. Each was genuinely interested in what the other said. Robert spoke of his plan to go to Mexico in the autumn, where fortune was waiting for him. He was always planning to go to Mexico, but somehow never got there. In the meantime he kept his modest position at a trading firm in New Orleans, where his equal command of English, French, and Spanish made him a valuable clerk and correspondent.

He spent his summer vacation, as he always did, with his mother at Grand Isle. In earlier times, before Robert could remember, the house had been a private summer retreat for the Lebruns. Now, with its dozen or more cottages always full of exclusive guests from the Quartier Français, it allowed Madame Lebrun to maintain the comfortable, unhurried life that seemed to be her birthright.

Mrs. Pontellier talked about her father’s plantation in Mississippi and her girlhood home in the old Kentucky bluegrass country. She was an American woman with a small trace of French that seemed to have been lost somewhere along the way. She read aloud a letter from her sister, who was away in the East and had just gotten engaged. Robert was interested and wanted to know what the sisters were like, what the father was like, and how long ago the mother had died.
When Mrs. Pontellier folded the letter, it was time to dress for the early dinner.
“I see Léonce isn’t coming back,” she said, glancing in the direction her husband had gone. Robert supposed not — there were quite a few New Orleans club men over at Klein’s.

When Mrs. Pontellier went inside to change, the young man came down the steps and wandered over to the croquet players, where he spent the half hour before dinner amusing himself with the little Pontellier boys, who were very fond of him.

chapters.title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: Mr. Pontellier returned from Klein’s hotel at eleven that night. He was in fine spirits, high energy, and very talkative. His arrival woke his wife, who had been deep asleep. He talked to her while he undressed, sharing anecdotes and bits of news and gossip he’d gathered through the day. From his trouser pockets he pulled a fistful of crumpled bills and a good deal of change, which he dumped on the bureau in a pile with his keys, pocketknife, handkerchief, and whatever else was in his pockets. She was heavy with sleep and answered him in murmurs.
He found it discouraging that his wife — the sole object of his existence — showed so little interest in things that concerned him, and put so little value on his conversation.

Mr. Pontellier had forgotten the bonbons and peanuts for the boys. He loved them dearly all the same, and went into the next room where they slept to check on them and make sure they were resting comfortably. What he found there was far from satisfactory. He shifted and turned the boys around in bed. One of them began to kick and mumble about a basket full of crabs.
Mr. Pontellier came back to his wife with the news that Raoul had a high fever and needed attention. Then he lit a cigar and went to sit near the open door to smoke it.

Mrs. Pontellier was quite sure Raoul had no fever. He had gone to bed perfectly well, she said, and had been fine all day. Mr. Pontellier knew fever symptoms too well to be mistaken. He told her the child was burning up in the next room at that very moment.

He accused his wife of inattention, of habitual neglect of the children. If it wasn’t a mother’s place to look after children, whose on earth was it? He himself was overwhelmed with his brokerage business. He couldn’t be in two places at once — earning a living for the family in the city, and staying home to make sure nothing went wrong. He spoke in a flat, relentless tone.

Mrs. Pontellier got out of bed and went into the next room. She came back shortly and sat on the edge of the bed, resting her head on the pillow. She said nothing, and refused to answer when her husband questioned her. When his cigar was done he went to bed, and within half a minute he was asleep.

By then Mrs. Pontellier was fully awake. She began to cry a little, wiping her eyes on the sleeve of her peignoir. She blew out the candle her husband had left burning, slipped her bare feet into a pair of satin mules at the foot of the bed, and went out onto the porch, where she sat in the wicker chair and began to rock slowly back and forth.

It was past midnight. The cottages were all dark. A single faint light showed from the hallway of the main house. No sound anywhere except the hooting of an old owl in a water oak, and the endless voice of the sea, which at that quiet hour seemed barely raised. It broke against the night like a mournful lullaby.

The tears came so fast that the damp sleeve of her peignoir was no longer enough to dry them. She was gripping the back of the chair with one hand; her loose sleeve had slipped nearly to her shoulder. She turned and pressed her wet, burning face into the crook of her arm, and went on crying there, not caring anymore to dry her face or her eyes or her arms. She couldn’t have said why she was crying. Such moments weren’t uncommon in her married life. They had never before seemed to count for much against the abundance of her husband’s kindness and the steady, unspoken devotion that had long since become taken for granted.

An indescribable heaviness, which seemed to rise from some unfamiliar place in her consciousness, filled her whole being with a vague anguish. It was like a shadow, like a mist drifting across the summer of her soul. Strange and unfamiliar — it was a mood. She wasn’t sitting there blaming her husband or raging at Fate for the life she’d been steered toward. She was simply crying, privately, for no reason she could name. The mosquitoes feasted on her, biting her firm round arms and nipping at her bare feet.
The little stinging, buzzing creatures managed to break a mood that might otherwise have kept her there in the dark for half the night.

The next morning Mr. Pontellier was up early to take the horse-drawn carriage to the steamboat at the wharf. He was going back to the city for work, and they wouldn’t see him again until the following Saturday. He had recovered his composure, which had seemed somewhat ruffled the night before. He was eager to be off, looking forward to a busy week on Carondelet Street.
Mr. Pontellier gave his wife half the money he had brought back from Klein’s the evening before. She liked money as well as most women, and accepted it with genuine pleasure.
“It’ll buy a lovely wedding present for Sister Janet!” she exclaimed, smoothing out the bills as she counted them.
“Oh, we’ll do better than that for Sister Janet, my dear,” he laughed, leaning in to kiss her goodbye.

The boys tumbled around him, grabbing at his legs, begging for all manner of things to be brought back. Mr. Pontellier was a great favorite — ladies, men, children, even the nurses, all came out to say goodbye to him. His wife stood smiling and waving, the boys calling out after him, as he disappeared in the old carriage down the sandy road.

A few days later a box arrived for Mrs. Pontellier from New Orleans. It was from her husband — packed with friandises, all manner of delicious things: the finest fruits, pâtés, a rare bottle or two, sweet syrups, and bonbons in abundance.

Mrs. Pontellier was always generous with such boxes; she was quite accustomed to receiving them when away from home. The pâtés and fruits were brought to the dining room; the bonbons were passed around. The ladies, selecting with delicate, eager fingers, all declared that Mr. Pontellier was the best husband in the world. Mrs. Pontellier was obliged to agree that she knew of none better.

chapters.title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: It would have been difficult for Mr. Pontellier to explain, to his own satisfaction or anyone else’s, exactly how his wife fell short in her duty toward their children. It was something he felt rather than perceived, and he never voiced it without regretting it afterward and making ample amends.

If one of the little Pontellier boys took a tumble while playing, he was unlikely to run crying to his mother — he would more probably pick himself up, wipe the water from his eyes and the sand from his mouth, and carry on. Young as they were, they stuck together and held their own in childish battles with fists raised and voices uplifted, and they generally won. The quadroon nurse was considered a great nuisance, useful only for buttoning up clothes and brushing and parting hair — since it appeared to be a law of society that hair must be parted and brushed.

In short, Mrs. Pontellier was not a mother-woman. The mother-women seemed to prevail that summer at Grand Isle. You could spot them easily, hovering with outstretched protective wings whenever any threat — real or imagined — approached their precious young. These were women who adored their children, worshipped their husbands, and considered it a sacred privilege to efface themselves as individuals and become ministering angels.

Many were splendid in the role; one of them was the very embodiment of womanly grace and charm. If her husband didn’t adore her, he was a brute who deserved a slow death. Her name was Adèle Ratignolle. No words describe her except the old ones that have done service for the heroine of romance and the fair lady of dreams. There was nothing subtle or hidden about her charms — her beauty was all there, brilliant and obvious: spun-gold hair that no comb or pin could contain; eyes that were nothing but sapphires; lips so deeply red you could only think of cherries or some other luscious crimson fruit. She was growing a little fuller, but it didn’t diminish by a fraction the grace of her every step, pose, and gesture. One would not have wished her white neck less full or her beautiful arms more slender. Never were hands more exquisite than hers, and it was a pleasure to watch them when she threaded her needle or fitted her gold thimble to her tapering middle finger as she sewed tiny night garments or shaped a bodice or a bib.

Madame Ratignolle was very fond of Mrs. Pontellier, and often brought her sewing over to sit with her in the afternoons. She was there the afternoon the box arrived from New Orleans. She had claimed the rocker and was busily sewing a tiny pair of nightdrawers.

She had brought the pattern for Mrs. Pontellier to cut out — a marvel of construction, designed to enclose a baby’s body so completely that only two small eyes could peer out, like an Eskimo. They were made for winter wear, when treacherous drafts came down chimneys and deadly cold crept through keyholes.

Mrs. Pontellier had no pressing concerns about her children’s current needs, and couldn’t see the point of spending summer afternoons thinking about winter nightgowns. But she didn’t want to seem unfriendly or uninterested, so she had laid out newspapers on the gallery floor and, following Madame Ratignolle’s directions, cut a pattern for the impervious garment.

Robert was there, seated as he’d been the Sunday before, and Mrs. Pontellier occupied the same spot on the upper step, leaning listlessly against the post. Beside her was a box of bonbons, which she held out to Madame Ratignolle from time to time.

That lady seemed unable to choose, but finally settled on a piece of nougat, wondering if it might not be too rich, whether it could possibly do her harm. Madame Ratignolle had been married seven years. Roughly every two years she had a baby. She had three children at that time and was beginning to think about a fourth. She was always mentioning her “condition.” Her condition was in no way visible, and no one would have suspected a thing had she not made it the constant subject of conversation.

Robert began to reassure her, saying he had known a woman who had subsisted on nougat throughout her entire — but noticing the color rise in Mrs. Pontellier’s face, he stopped himself and changed the subject.

Mrs. Pontellier, though she had married a Creole, was not entirely comfortable in Creole society; she had never before been thrown so closely among them. That summer at Lebrun’s the guests were all Creoles. They all knew each other and moved like one large family, bound by easy goodwill. What struck Mrs. Pontellier most forcibly was their complete absence of prudishness. Their freedom of expression was at first incomprehensible to her, though she had no difficulty reconciling it with the profound chastity that in Creole women seems inborn and unmistakable.

Edna Pontellier would never forget the shock of hearing Madame Ratignolle tell old Monsieur Farival the harrowing story of one of her accouchements, sparing no intimate detail. She was growing used to such shocks, but she still couldn’t keep the color from rising in her cheeks. More than once her arrival had interrupted some ribald story Robert was telling to a group of amused married women.

A book had circulated through the pension. When it was Edna’s turn to read it, she did so with profound astonishment. She felt compelled to read it in secret and solitude — though none of the others had bothered — hiding it at the sound of approaching footsteps. It was discussed openly and freely at table. Mrs. Pontellier gave up being astonished and concluded that wonders would never cease.

chapters.title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: They made a congenial group that summer afternoon — Madame Ratignolle sewing steadily, often pausing to tell a story with much expressive movement of her beautiful hands; Robert and Mrs. Pontellier sitting idle, trading occasional words, glances, or smiles that indicated a certain settled intimacy and ease.

He had kept close to her during the past month. No one thought anything of it. Many had predicted that Robert would attach himself to Mrs. Pontellier when he arrived. Since the age of fifteen — eleven years before — Robert had each summer at Grand Isle devoted himself to some attractive woman. Sometimes it was a young girl, sometimes a widow, but as often as not a married woman who interested him.

For two consecutive seasons he had lived in the reflected light of Mademoiselle Duvigné’s presence. But she died between summers; then Robert cast himself as inconsolable, prostrating himself at the feet of Madame Ratignolle for whatever crumbs of sympathy and comfort she saw fit to bestow.
Mrs. Pontellier liked to sit and look at her radiant companion the way one might contemplate a flawless Madonna.

“Can anyone fathom the cruelty beneath that beautiful exterior?” murmured Robert. “She knew that I adored her once, and she let me adore her. It was ‘Robert, come; go; stand up; sit down; do this; do that; check if the baby is sleeping; my thimble, please, I left it God knows where. Come and read Daudet to me while I sew.’”
“Par exemple! I never had to ask. You were always under my feet, like a troublesome cat.”
“You mean like an adoring dog. And the moment Ratignolle appeared on the scene, it was like a dog. ‘Passéz! Adieu! Allez vous-en!’”

“Perhaps I feared to make Alphonse jealous,” she said, with exaggerated innocence. That made them all laugh. The right hand jealous of the left! The heart jealous of the soul! But in any case, the Creole husband is never jealous — with him that corroding passion has withered from disuse.

Meanwhile Robert, addressing Mrs. Pontellier, went on telling of his former hopeless passion for Madame Ratignolle — of sleepless nights, of consuming flames, until the very sea sizzled when he took his daily swim. While the lady at her needlework kept up a running, dismissive commentary:
“Blagueur — farceur — gros bête, va!”

He never took this mock-serious tone when alone with Mrs. Pontellier. She never quite knew what to make of it; at that moment it was impossible to judge how much was jest and how much was earnest. It was understood that he had often spoken words of love to Madame Ratignolle without any expectation of being taken seriously. Mrs. Pontellier was glad he had assumed no similar role with her. It would have been unwelcome and irritating.
Mrs. Pontellier had brought her sketching things, which she played with in an amateur way. She liked the dabbling. It gave her a particular kind of satisfaction that nothing else could.

She had long wanted to try Madame Ratignolle as a subject. Never had that lady seemed a more tempting model than at this moment — seated there like some sensuous Madonna, the glow of the fading day enriching her vivid coloring.

Robert moved across and sat on the step below Mrs. Pontellier, to watch her work. She handled her brushes with ease and assurance that came not from long practice but from natural aptitude. Robert followed her work closely, murmuring little exclamations of approval in French, addressed to Madame Ratignolle.
“Mais ce n’est pas mal! Elle s’y connaît, elle a de la force, oui.”

Lost in watching, he once quietly rested his head against Mrs. Pontellier’s arm. She pushed him away gently. He did it again. She was inclined to think it was thoughtlessness on his part, but that was no reason to tolerate it. She said nothing — simply pushed him away again, quietly but firmly. He didn’t apologize. The finished portrait bore no resemblance to Madame Ratignolle. That lady was greatly disappointed. But the sketch was decent enough work, satisfying in many respects.
Mrs. Pontellier evidently didn’t think so. After looking at it critically, she drew a broad smear of paint across the surface and crumpled the paper in her hands.

The children came tumbling up the steps, the quadroon nurse following at the respectful distance they required of her. Mrs. Pontellier sent them to carry her paints and things inside. She tried to keep them for a moment of conversation and play, but they were on a mission. They had come only to investigate the bonbon box. They accepted whatever she gave them without complaint, each holding out two chubby cupped hands in the vain hope of getting more, and then they were off.

The sun was low in the west, and a soft, languid breeze came up from the south, carrying the faint, seductive smell of the sea. Children freshly dressed were gathering under the oaks for their evening games. Their voices were high and piercing.

Madame Ratignolle folded her sewing, tucking thimble, scissors, and thread neatly into a roll, which she pinned shut. She complained of faintness. Mrs. Pontellier hurried for cologne water and a fan. She bathed Madame Ratignolle’s face with the cologne while Robert plied the fan with excessive energy.
The spell passed quickly, and Mrs. Pontellier couldn’t help wondering whether there hadn’t been a little imagination behind it — for the rose color had never left her friend’s face.

She watched the lovely woman move down the long gallery with the grace and majesty sometimes attributed to queens. Her little ones ran to meet her. Two clung to her white skirts; the third she lifted from the nurse and carried, with a thousand endearments, in her own encircling arms. Though, as everyone well knew, the doctor had forbidden her to lift so much as a pin!
“Are you going swimming?” Robert asked Mrs. Pontellier. It was more reminder than question.
“Oh, no,” she answered, with a note of hesitation. “I’m tired; I don’t think so.” Her gaze drifted from his face toward the gulf, whose deep murmur reached her like a loving but insistent summons.
“Come on!” he pressed. “You can’t miss your swim. The water must be wonderful; it won’t hurt you. Come.”

He reached up for her big, rough straw hat hanging on a peg outside the door and put it on her head. They went down the steps and walked together toward the beach. The sun was low in the west, and the breeze was soft and warm.

chapters.title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: Edna Pontellier could not have said why, having wished to go to the beach with Robert, she had first declined, and then gone — obeying one of the two contradictory impulses that pulled at her.
A certain light was beginning to dawn inside her — the kind of light that, while showing the way, also forbids it.

At that early stage it only confused her. It stirred in her an inclination toward dreams, toward a pensive stillness, toward the shadowy anguish that had overtaken her at midnight when she had given herself over to tears.

In short, Mrs. Pontellier was beginning to grasp her position in the universe as a human being, and to recognize her relationship — as an individual — to the world within and around her. This may seem a ponderous weight of wisdom to settle upon the soul of a young woman of twenty-eight — perhaps more wisdom than is usually granted to any woman.

But the beginning of things, especially of a world, is necessarily vague, tangled, chaotic, and deeply unsettling. How few of us make it through such beginnings. How many souls are lost in the upheaval.
The voice of the sea is seductive — never silent, whispering, insisting, murmuring, inviting the soul to wander awhile in abysses of solitude, to lose itself in labyrinths of inner contemplation.
The voice of the sea speaks to the soul. The touch of the sea is sensuous, enfolding the body in its soft, close embrace.

chapters.title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: Mrs. Pontellier was not a woman given to confidences — this was contrary to her nature. Even as a child she had lived entirely within herself. From an early age she had instinctively understood the dual life — the outward existence that conforms, the inner life that questions.

That summer at Grand Isle she began to loosen a little the cloak of reserve she had always worn. There may have been — there must have been — influences both subtle and obvious working on her, but the most immediate was the influence of Adèle Ratignolle. The Creole woman’s overwhelming physical charm first attracted her, since Edna had a sensuous susceptibility to beauty. Then the complete transparency of the woman’s existence — readable by anyone, forming such a striking contrast to Edna’s own habitual reserve — this may have been the link. Who can say what metals the gods use to forge the bond we call sympathy, which we might as well call love.

The two women walked out one morning to the beach together, arm in arm, under the large white sunshade. Edna had persuaded Madame Ratignolle to leave the children behind, though she couldn’t get her to surrender a small roll of needlework, which Adèle begged to slip into the depths of her pocket. By some means they had gotten away from Robert.

The walk to the beach was no small undertaking, along a long sandy path where straggling growth on either side kept breaking in and narrowing the way. Acres of yellow chamomile spread out on both sides. Farther still, vegetable gardens stretched out, with here and there plantations of orange and lemon trees. The dark clusters of leaves gleamed in the sunlight from a distance.

Both women were tall, Madame Ratignolle with the fuller, more maternal figure. The charm of Edna Pontellier’s build crept up on you quietly. Her lines were long, clean, and symmetrical; hers was a body that fell sometimes into splendid attitudes; there was nothing of the stiff, fashionable figure about it. A passing stranger might not look twice. But with finer feeling and perception he would have recognized the noble beauty of its form, and the graceful severity of her poise and movement, which set Edna Pontellier apart.

That morning she wore a cool white muslin with a waving vertical stripe of brown running through it, a white linen collar, and the big straw hat taken from the peg outside the door. The hat sat any which way on her brownish-yellow hair, which waved slightly and lay heavy and close against her head.

Madame Ratignolle, more careful of her complexion, had wrapped a gauze veil about her head and wore dogskin gloves with wide gauntlets to protect her wrists. She was all in white, with a flounce of ruffles that became her. The soft, drapey things she wore suited her lush, full beauty in a way that anything more severe could not.

There were a number of bathhouses along the beach — rough but solid structures, each with a small covered gallery facing the water. Each house had two compartments, and each family at Lebrun’s claimed one for itself, fitted out with bathing necessities and whatever personal comforts the owners wished. The two women had no intention of bathing; they had simply walked down to be near the water and to be alone. The Pontellier and Ratignolle compartments were side by side under the same roof.

Mrs. Pontellier had brought her key out of habit. She unlocked her bathhouse door, went inside, and came back out carrying a rug, which she spread on the gallery floor, and two large hair-stuffed pillows, which she leaned against the front wall of the building.

They settled in the shade of the gallery, sitting side by side against the pillows with their feet stretched out. Madame Ratignolle removed her veil, dabbed at her face with a delicate handkerchief, and fanned herself with the fan she always carried on a long ribbon somewhere about her person. Edna removed her collar and opened the neck of her dress. She took the fan from Madame Ratignolle and began to fan them both. It was very warm, and for a while they did nothing but remark on the heat, the sun, the glare. But there was a choppy, stiff wind off the water that whipped the sea to froth. It made their skirts flutter and kept them busy adjusting, readjusting, tucking in, securing hairpins and hatpins. A few people were swimming some distance off. The beach was quiet at that hour. The woman in black was reading her morning prayers on the gallery of a neighboring bathhouse. Two young lovers were exchanging their hearts’ yearnings beneath the children’s tent, which they had found vacant.

Edna Pontellier, looking around, finally brought her gaze to rest on the sea. The day was clear, carrying the eye as far as the blue sky went; a few white clouds hung lazily over the horizon. A lateen sail was visible in the direction of Cat Island; others to the south seemed almost motionless in the far distance.

“Of whom — of what are you thinking?” asked Adèle, who had been watching her companion’s face with quiet, amused attention, struck by the absorbed look that had fixed every feature into a kind of stillness.

“Nothing,” said Mrs. Pontellier with a start, adding at once: “How absurd! But it does seem to be the reply one makes instinctively to that question. Let me see,” she went on, tilting her head back and narrowing her eyes until they shone like two bright points of light. “Let me see. I wasn’t really thinking of anything at all — but perhaps I can trace my thoughts.”
“Oh, never mind!” laughed Madame Ratignolle. “I’m not that demanding. I’ll excuse you this time. It really is too hot to think — especially to think about thinking.”

“But for the fun of it,” Edna persisted. “First of all, looking at the water stretching so far away, those still sails against the blue sky — it made such a beautiful picture I simply wanted to sit and look. And the hot wind in my face made me think — with no connection I can trace — of a summer day in Kentucky, of a meadow that seemed as big as the ocean to the small girl walking through it, the grass higher than her waist. She threw her arms out like a swimmer as she walked, batting through the tall grass as if striking through water. Oh, I see the connection now!”
“Where were you going that day in Kentucky, walking through the grass?”

“I don’t remember now. I was just walking diagonally across a big field. My sunbonnet blocked the view. All I could see was the stretch of green in front of me, and I felt as if I had to keep walking forever, as if there were no end to it. I don’t remember whether I was frightened or pleased. I must have been happy.”
“I daresay it was Sunday,” she laughed, “and I was running away from prayers — from the Presbyterian service my father read in such a spirit of gloom it still chills me to think of.”
“And have you been running away from prayers ever since, ma chère?” asked Madame Ratignolle, amused.

“No! Oh, no!” Edna said quickly. “I was a thoughtless child then, just following impulse without reflection. On the contrary, there was a period of my life when religion took a real hold on me — from about twelve until — until — well, I suppose until now, though I’ve never really thought about it, just drifting along by habit. But do you know,” she broke off, turning her quick eyes on Madame Ratignolle and leaning forward until their faces were close together, “sometimes this summer I feel as if I’m walking through that green meadow again — idly, aimlessly, with nothing guiding me and nothing pulling me anywhere in particular.”

Madame Ratignolle laid her hand over Mrs. Pontellier’s, which was near her. Seeing it was not withdrawn, she clasped it warmly and firmly. She even stroked it a little, softly, with her other hand, murmuring under her breath: “Pauvre chérie.”

The gesture was at first slightly startling to Edna, but she soon relaxed into the Creole’s gentle caress. She was unaccustomed to open, spoken expressions of affection — in herself or in others. She and her younger sister Janet had quarreled a great deal through long-standing habit. Her older sister Margaret was matronly and composed, probably from having taken on housewifely responsibilities too young — their mother had died when they were all quite small. Margaret was not demonstrative; she was practical. Edna had had occasional friends, but whether by chance or otherwise, they had all seemed to be of one kind — self-contained. She never realized that her own reserved nature had perhaps everything to do with this. Her closest friend at school had been a girl of exceptional intellectual gifts, who wrote fine-sounding essays that Edna admired and tried to imitate; together they had talked heatedly about the English classics, and sometimes argued religion and politics.

Edna had long wondered at one tendency that sometimes disturbed her inwardly without ever showing itself outwardly. Very early — perhaps when she was walking through the ocean of waving grass — she remembered being passionately taken with a handsome, sad-eyed cavalry officer who visited her father in Kentucky. She couldn’t leave his presence when he was there, or take her eyes from his face, which was something like Napoleon’s, with a lock of black hair falling across the forehead. But the cavalry officer faded, imperceptibly, out of her life.

At another time her feelings were deeply engaged by a young man who came visiting at a plantation near theirs, after the family had moved to Mississippi. He was engaged to the young lady there, and they sometimes called on Margaret, driving over in a buggy on afternoons. Edna was a girl just entering her teens, and the realization that she herself was nothing — nothing, nothing — to this engaged young man was a sharp and bitter hurt. But he, too, went the way of dreams.

She was grown when she was overtaken by what she believed to be the great passion of her life. It was when the face and figure of a celebrated tragedian began to haunt her imagination and stir her senses. The persistence of the feeling gave it an air of genuineness. Its very hopelessness colored it with the elevated tones of a grand passion.

A portrait of the tragedian stood framed on her desk. Anyone might keep a tragedian’s photograph without exciting comment or suspicion. (This was a thought she cherished with some dark satisfaction.) In company she spoke admiringly of his exalted gifts, passing the photograph around and dwelling on the likeness. Alone, she would sometimes pick it up and kiss the cold glass with feeling.

Her marriage to Léonce Pontellier had been, in this sense, an accident — like many marriages that present themselves as the decrees of Fate. It was in the midst of her secret great passion that she met him. He fell in love in the way men are accustomed to doing, and pressed his suit with an earnestness and ardor that left nothing lacking. He pleased her; his total devotion flattered her. She imagined they shared a sympathy of mind and taste — in which she was mistaken. Add to this the fierce opposition of her father and sister Margaret to her marrying a Catholic, and one need look no further for why she accepted Monsieur Pontellier.

The perfect happiness that a marriage to the tragedian would have been was not for her in this world. As the devoted wife of a man who worshipped her, she felt she would take her place with a certain dignity in the real world, closing forever the door on the realm of romance and dreams.

But it was not long before the tragedian had joined the cavalry officer and the engaged young man and a handful of others; and Edna found herself face to face with ordinary life. She grew fond of her husband, recognizing with some quiet satisfaction that no trace of passion or excessive invented warmth colored her affection — which therefore wasn’t in danger of dissolving.

She loved her children in an uneven, impulsive way. Sometimes she would gather them to her heart with passionate tenderness; sometimes she would forget them. The year before, they had spent part of the summer with their grandmother Pontellier in Iberville. Feeling secure that they were well cared for and happy, she didn’t miss them except in occasional intense bursts. Their absence was, in some way, a relief — though she didn’t admit this, even to herself. It seemed to free her from a responsibility she had taken on blindly, and for which she was not fitted.

Edna did not reveal all of this to Madame Ratignolle that summer afternoon with their faces turned toward the sea. But a good deal of it escaped her. She had rested her head on Madame Ratignolle’s shoulder. She was flushed and felt almost intoxicated by the sound of her own voice and the unaccustomed taste of candor. It confused her pleasantly, like wine, or like a first breath of freedom.

The sound of approaching voices. It was Robert, with a group of children, searching for them. The two little Pontelliers were with him, and he carried Madame Ratignolle’s small daughter in his arms. Other children followed, with two nurses bringing up the rear, looking resigned and put-upon.

The women at once got up and began shaking out their clothes and stretching their limbs. Mrs. Pontellier threw the cushions and rug back into the bathhouse. The children all rushed to the tent, where they stood in a line staring at the two young lovers who were still exchanging their vows and sighs. The lovers rose without much protest and drifted quietly away elsewhere.
The children took possession of the tent, and Mrs. Pontellier went over to join them.
Madame Ratignolle asked Robert to walk her back to the house; she complained of cramp in her legs and stiffness in her joints. She leaned heavily on his arm as they walked.

chapters.title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: “Do me a favor, Robert,” said the pretty woman at his side, almost as soon as they had set off homeward. She looked up at his face, leaning on his arm in the shadow of the umbrella he had raised.
“Granted — as many as you like,” he answered, glancing down at her eyes, which were full of thought and something like calculation.
“Just one: leave Mrs. Pontellier alone.”
“Tiens!” he exclaimed, with a sudden boyish laugh. “Voilà que Madame Ratignolle est jalouse!”
“Nonsense! I’m serious; I mean what I say. Leave Mrs. Pontellier alone.”
“Why?” he asked, growing serious at his companion’s insistence.
“She is not one of us; she is not like us. She might make the unfortunate mistake of taking you seriously.”

His face flushed with annoyance, and pulling off his soft hat he began to beat it impatiently against his leg as he walked. “Why shouldn’t she take me seriously?” he demanded sharply. “Am I a comedian, a clown, a fool? Why shouldn’t she? You Creoles! I have no patience with you! Am I always to be treated as part of the entertainment? I hope Mrs. Pontellier does take me seriously. I hope she has the discernment to find something in me besides the blagueur. If I thought there was any doubt —”

“Oh, enough, Robert!” she broke in. “You’re not thinking about what you’re saying. You speak with about as much reflection as one of those children playing in the sand. If your attentions to any married woman here were ever intended to be convincing, you would not be the gentleman we all know you to be, and you would be unfit to associate with the wives and daughters of people who trust you.”
Madame Ratignolle had spoken what she believed to be law and gospel. The young man shrugged his shoulders impatiently.
“Oh, well! That’s not the point,” he said, slamming his hat back on his head. “You ought to feel that such things are not flattering to say to a fellow.”
“Should our entire relationship consist of exchanging compliments? Ma foi!”

“It isn’t pleasant to have a woman tell you —” he went on, but breaking off suddenly: “Now if I were like Arobin — you remember Alcée Arobin and that story about the consul’s wife at Biloxi?” And he told the story of Alcée Arobin and the consul’s wife, and another about the tenor at the French Opera who received letters he should never have received, and other stories, comic and serious, until Mrs. Pontellier and her possible tendency to take young men seriously was apparently forgotten.

Madame Ratignolle, when they reached her cottage, went in to take the hour’s rest she considered good for her health. Before leaving her, Robert asked her pardon for the impatience — he called it rudeness — with which he had received her well-meant warning.

“You made one mistake, Adèle,” he said, with an easy smile. “There is absolutely no possibility of Mrs. Pontellier ever taking me seriously. You should have warned me against taking myself seriously. Your advice might then have carried some weight and given me something to think about. Au revoir. But you look tired,” he added, with concern. “Would you like a cup of bouillon? Shall I make you a toddy? Let me mix you a toddy with a dash of Angostura.”

She agreed to the bouillon, which was welcome and satisfying. He went himself to the kitchen — a separate building to the rear of the house — and himself brought her the golden-brown bouillon in a delicate Sèvres cup, with a flaky cracker or two on the saucer.

She put out a bare white arm from the curtain across her open door and took the cup from him. She told him he was a bon garçon, and she meant it. Robert thanked her and turned away toward the main house.

The lovers were just entering the pension grounds. They leaned toward each other the way the water oaks bent toward the sea. There was not a particle of earth beneath their feet. Their heads might have been turned upside down, so completely did they move through pure blue air. The woman in black, creeping behind them, looked a shade paler and more worn than usual. There was no sign of Mrs. Pontellier and the children. Robert scanned the distance for any sign of them. They would doubtless stay away until dinnertime. The young man went up to his mother’s room at the top of the house, fitted together from odd angles under a sloping ceiling. Two broad dormer windows looked out over the Gulf, as far across as an eye could reach. The furnishings were light, cool, and practical.
Madame Lebrun was busy at the sewing machine. A little black girl sat on the floor working the treadle with her hands. The Creole woman takes no unnecessary chances with her health.

Robert went and settled himself on the broad windowsill. He took a book from his pocket and began reading it with great apparent energy, judging by how often and precisely he turned the pages. The sewing machine made a tremendous clatter in the room — it was an old, ponderous model. In the lulls, Robert and his mother exchanged bits of scattered conversation.
“Where is Mrs. Pontellier?”
“Down at the beach with the children.”
“I promised to lend her the Goncourt. Don’t forget to take it down when you go; it’s there on the shelf above the small table.” Clatter, clatter, clatter, bang! — for the next five or eight minutes.
“Where is Victor going with the carriage?”
“The carriage? Victor?”
“Yes — down there in front. He seems to be getting ready to drive somewhere.”
“Call him.” Clatter, clatter!
Robert let out a shrill, piercing whistle that could have been heard all the way to the wharf.
Madame Lebrun flew to the window. She called “Victor!” She waved her handkerchief and called again. The young man below got into the vehicle and started the horse at a gallop.
Madame Lebrun went back to the machine, crimson with annoyance. Victor was the younger son — hot-headed, with a temper that invited violence and a will no one could break.
“Whenever you give the word, I’m ready to knock some sense into him.”

“If only your father had lived!” Clatter, clatter, clatter, clatter, bang! It was Madame Lebrun’s firm conviction that the universe and everything in it would have been managed with decidedly more intelligence and order had not Monsieur Lebrun been taken away during the early years of their married life.

“What do you hear from Montel?” Montel was a middle-aged gentleman whose vain ambition for the past twenty years had been to fill the void left by Monsieur Lebrun’s death in the Lebrun household. Clatter, clatter, bang, clatter!

“I have a letter somewhere,” she said, rummaging in the sewing-machine drawer and finding it at the bottom of the workbasket. “He says to tell you he’ll be in Vera Cruz early next month —” clatter, clatter! “— and if you still intend to join him —” bang! clatter, clatter, bang!
“Why didn’t you tell me sooner, mother? You know I wanted —” Clatter, clatter, clatter!
“Do you see Mrs. Pontellier coming back with the children? She’ll be late for lunch again. She never starts to get ready until the last minute.” Clatter, clatter! “Where are you going?”
“Where did you say the Goncourt was?”

chapters.title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: Every light in the hall was ablaze; every lamp turned as high as it could go without smoking the chimney or threatening explosion. The lamps were fixed at intervals against the walls, encircling the whole room. Someone had gathered orange and lemon branches and fashioned graceful garlands between them. The dark green of the branches stood out against the white muslin curtains that draped the windows, puffing and flapping in the capricious gusts of a stiff breeze sweeping up from the Gulf.

It was Saturday night, a few weeks after the intimate conversation between Robert and Madame Ratignolle on the walk from the beach. An unusual number of husbands, fathers, and friends had come down to stay over Sunday, and they were being properly entertained by their families, with Madame Lebrun's help. The dining tables had been moved to one end of the hall, and the chairs arranged in rows and clusters. Each little family group had shared its news and domestic gossip earlier in the evening. Now there was a general inclination to relax, to widen the circle and turn the conversation more general.

Many of the children had been permitted to stay up past their usual bedtime. A small group of them lay on their stomachs on the floor, looking at the colored comic pages Mr. Pontellier had brought down. The little Pontellier boys were overseeing them and making their authority felt.
Music, dancing, and a recitation or two were the entertainments provided — or rather, offered. But there was nothing organized about the program, no air of prearrangement or even premeditation.

Early in the evening the Farival twins were persuaded to play the piano. They were girls of fourteen, always dressed in the Virgin’s colors, blue and white, having been dedicated to the Blessed Virgin at their baptism. They played a duet from Zampa, and at the earnest request of everyone present followed it with the overture to The Poet and the Peasant.

“Allez vous-en! Sapristi!” shrieked the parrot outside the door. He was the only creature present with enough candor to admit that he had heard these gracious performances more than once before this summer. Old Monsieur Farival, grandfather of the twins, grew indignant at the interruption and insisted the bird be removed and confined to darkness. Victor Lebrun objected, and his decrees were as immutable as fate. The parrot fortunately offered no further interruption to the entertainment — apparently all the venom in his nature had been used up in that one outburst against the twins.
Later a young brother and sister gave recitations that everyone present had heard many times at winter parties in the city.

A little girl danced a skirt dance in the center of the floor. Her mother played the accompaniment and watched her daughter with eager admiration and nervous worry. There was no need for worry. The child was mistress of the situation. She had been properly dressed for the occasion in black tulle and black silk tights. Her little neck and arms were bare, and her hair, artificially crimped, stood out around her head like fluffy black plumes. Her poses were full of grace, and her little black-shod toes flashed as they shot out and upward with a speed and suddenness that was dazzling.

But there was no reason why everyone shouldn’t dance. Madame Ratignolle could not, so she cheerfully agreed to play for the others. She played very well, keeping excellent waltz time and putting a spirit into the music that was genuinely inspiring. She was keeping up her playing for the sake of the children, she said; because she and her husband both saw it as a way of brightening the home and making it pleasant.

Almost everyone danced except the twins, who could not be induced to separate during the brief period when one or the other might be whirling around the room in a man’s arms. They might have danced together, but it didn’t occur to them.

The children were sent to bed. Some went obediently; others went with shrieks and protests as they were carried away. They had been permitted to stay up until after the ice cream, which naturally marked the limit of human indulgence.

Ice cream was passed around with cake — gold and silver cake arranged on platters in alternate slices; it had been made and frozen that afternoon behind the kitchen by two black women, under Victor’s supervision. It was declared a great success — excellent if it had only had a little less vanilla or a little more sugar, if it had been frozen a degree harder, and if the salt might have been kept out of certain portions. Victor was proud of his achievement and went about recommending it and urging everyone to have more.

After Mrs. Pontellier had danced twice with her husband, once with Robert, and once with Monsieur Ratignolle — who was thin and tall and swayed like a reed in the wind when he danced — she went out onto the gallery and sat on the low window sill, from which she could see everything going on in the hall and look out toward the Gulf. There was a soft glow in the east. The moon was coming up, its mystic shimmer casting a million lights across the distant, restless water.

“Would you like to hear Mademoiselle Reisz play?” asked Robert, coming out onto the gallery where she sat. Of course Edna would like to hear Mademoiselle Reisz play; but she feared it would be useless to ask her.

“I’ll ask her,” he said. “I’ll tell her you want to hear her. She likes you. She’ll come.” He turned and hurried away to one of the far cottages, where Mademoiselle Reisz was shuffling about — dragging a chair in and out of her room, and at intervals objecting to the crying of a baby in the adjoining cottage that a nurse was trying to put to sleep. She was a disagreeable little woman, no longer young, who had quarreled with almost everyone, owing to a temper that was self-assertive and a habit of trampling on the rights of others. Robert persuaded her without too much difficulty.

She entered the hall with him during a lull in the dancing. She made an awkward, imperious little bow as she went in. She was a plain woman, with a small, wizened face and body and eyes that burned. She had absolutely no taste in dress and wore a collection of rusty black lace with a bunch of artificial violets pinned to the side of her hair.

“Ask Mrs. Pontellier what she would like me to play,” she requested of Robert. She sat perfectly still before the piano, not touching the keys, while Robert carried her message to Edna at the window. A general air of surprise and genuine satisfaction fell upon everyone as they saw the pianist enter. There was a settling down, and a prevailing air of expectancy. Edna was a little embarrassed at being singled out for the imperious little woman’s attention. She would not dare to choose, and asked that Mademoiselle Reisz please herself in her selections.

Edna was what she herself called very fond of music. Well-played music had a way of evoking pictures in her mind. She sometimes liked to sit in the room of mornings when Madame Ratignolle played or practiced. One piece that lady played Edna had named “Solitude.” It was a short, plaintive, minor melody. The piece had another name, but she called it “Solitude.” When she heard it, there rose before her imagination the figure of a man standing beside a desolate rock on the seashore. He was naked. His attitude was one of hopeless resignation as he looked toward a distant bird winging its flight away from him.

Another piece called to her mind a graceful young woman in an Empire gown, taking mincing dancing steps as she came down a long avenue between tall hedges. Again, another reminded her of children at play, and still another of nothing on earth but a demure lady stroking a cat.

The very first chords that Mademoiselle Reisz struck upon the piano sent a keen tremor down Mrs. Pontellier’s spine. It was not the first time she had heard an artist at the piano. Perhaps it was the first time she was ready; perhaps the first time her being was open to receive an impression of lasting truth.

She waited for the mental pictures that she thought would gather and blaze before her imagination. She waited in vain. She saw no pictures of solitude, of hope, of longing, or of despair. But the passions themselves were aroused within her soul, swaying it, lashing it, as the waves beat daily upon her splendid body. She trembled, she was choking, and the tears blinded her.
Mademoiselle Reisz had finished. She arose, and with her stiff, lofty bow, went away, stopping for neither thanks nor applause. As she passed along the gallery she patted Edna upon the shoulder.

“Well, how did you like my music?” she asked. The young woman was unable to answer; she pressed the pianist’s hand convulsively. Mademoiselle Reisz saw her agitation and even her tears. She patted her again upon the shoulder as she said:
“You are the only one worth playing for. Those others? Bah!” And she went shuffling and sidling on down the gallery toward her room.

But she was wrong about “those others.” Her playing had aroused a fever of enthusiasm. “What passion!” “What an artist!” “I have always said no one could play Chopin like Mademoiselle Reisz!” “That last prelude! Bon Dieu! It shakes a man!”
It was growing late, and there was a general move to break up. But someone — perhaps it was Robert — thought of a swim at that mystic hour and under that mystic moon.

chapters.title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: At all events Robert proposed it, and there was not a dissenting voice. Every one was ready to follow when he led the way. He did not lead the way, however; he directed the way. He himself lingered behind with the lovers, who had shown a disposition to stay apart. He walked between them, whether with mischievous or malicious intent was not entirely clear, even to himself.

The Pontelliers and Ratignolles walked ahead, the women leaning on their husbands’ arms. Edna could hear Robert’s voice behind them, and sometimes make out what he was saying. She wondered why he didn’t join them. It was unlike him. Lately he had sometimes stayed away from her for an entire day, redoubling his attentiveness the next day and the day after, as if making up for lost hours. She missed him on the days when some excuse took him away, the way one misses the sun on a cloudy day without having thought much about the sun when it was shining.

The group walked in little clusters toward the beach. They talked and laughed; some sang. Music drifted up faintly from Klein’s hotel, mellowed by the distance. Strange, rare scents were in the air — a mingling of sea and weeds and damp newly-turned earth, mixed with the heavy perfume of a field of white blossoms somewhere nearby. The night lay lightly on the sea and land. There was no weight of darkness; there were no shadows. The white light of the moon had fallen upon the world like the mystery and softness of sleep.

Most of them walked into the water as though entering their natural element. The sea was quiet now, swelling lazily in broad, smooth billows that melted into one another and did not break except on the beach in little foamy crests that curled back like slow white serpents.

Edna had spent the entire summer trying to learn to swim. She had received instructions from the men and the women; in some instances from the children. Robert had conducted almost daily lessons, and was nearly at the point of giving up, feeling his efforts were futile. A certain uncontrollable fear overtook her in the water unless there was a hand close by to reach out and steady her.

But that night she was like the little tottering, stumbling, clutching child who suddenly realizes its power and walks alone for the first time, boldly and with over-confidence. She could have shouted for joy. She did shout for joy, as with a sweeping stroke or two she lifted her body to the surface of the water.

A feeling of exultation overtook her, as if some power of great import had been given her — to control the working of her body and her soul. She grew daring and reckless, overestimating her strength. She wanted to swim far out, where no woman had swum before.
Her unexpected achievement was the subject of wonder, applause, and admiration. Each person congratulated themselves that their own particular lessons had brought about this happy result.

“How easy it is!” she thought. “It is nothing,” she said aloud; “why did I not discover before that it was nothing. Think of the time I have lost splashing about like a baby!” She would not join the groups in their games and play, but, intoxicated with her newly conquered power, she swam out alone.

She turned her face toward the open sea to take in an impression of space and solitude, which the vast expanse of water, melting into the moonlit sky, conveyed to her excited mind. As she swam she seemed to be reaching out for something unlimited in which to lose herself.

Once she turned and looked back toward the shore, toward the people she had left there. She had not gone any great distance — what would have been a great distance for an experienced swimmer. But to her unaccustomed eyes the stretch of water behind her seemed like a barrier that her own strength could never overcome.
A quick vision of death struck her soul, and for a moment appalled and enfeebled her senses. But by an effort she rallied her faltering faculties and managed to regain the land.
She made no mention of her encounter with death and her flash of terror, except to say to her husband, “I thought I should have perished out there alone.”
“You were not so very far, my dear; I was watching you,” he told her.

Edna went at once to the bathhouse, and she had put on her dry clothes and was ready to return home before the others had left the water. She started to walk away alone. They all called to her and shouted to her. She waved a dismissing hand, and went on, paying no further heed to their renewed cries seeking to detain her.
“Sometimes I am tempted to think that Mrs. Pontellier is capricious,” said Madame Lebrun, who was enjoying herself enormously and feared that Edna’s abrupt departure might put an end to the fun.
“I know she is,” agreed Mr. Pontellier; “sometimes, not often.”
Edna had not gone a quarter of the way home before Robert overtook her.
“Did you think I was afraid?” she asked him, without a trace of annoyance.
“No; I knew you weren’t afraid.”
“Then why did you come? Why didn’t you stay out there with the others?”
“I never thought of it.”
“Of anything. What difference does it make?”
“I’m very tired,” she said, with a note of complaint.

“You don’t know anything about it. Why should you know? I’ve never been so exhausted in my life. But it isn’t unpleasant. A thousand emotions have swept through me tonight. I don’t understand half of them. Don’t mind what I’m saying; I’m just thinking aloud. I wonder if anything will ever move me again the way Mademoiselle Reisz’s playing moved me tonight. I wonder if any night on earth will ever be like this one. It is like a night in a dream. The people around me are like strange, half-human beings. There must be spirits abroad tonight.”
“There are,” whispered Robert. “Didn’t you know this was the twenty-eighth of August?”
“The twenty-eighth of August?”

“Yes. On the twenty-eighth of August, at the hour of midnight, and if the moon is shining — the moon must be shining — a spirit that has haunted these shores for ages rises up from the Gulf. With its own penetrating vision the spirit seeks some mortal worthy to keep it company, worthy of being exalted for a few hours into the realm of the semi-celestial. Its search has always hitherto been fruitless, and it has sunk back, disheartened, into the sea. But tonight it found Mrs. Pontellier. Perhaps it will never wholly release her from the spell. Perhaps she will never again suffer a poor, unworthy earthling to walk in the shadow of her divine presence.”

“Don’t tease me,” she said, wounded by what seemed to be his flippancy. He did not heed the entreaty, but the tone — with its delicate note of pain — was like a reproach. He could not explain; he could not tell her that he had penetrated her mood and understood. He said nothing except to offer her his arm, for, by her own admission, she was exhausted. She had been walking alone with her arms hanging limp, letting her white skirts trail along the dewy path. She took his arm, but she did not lean upon it. She let her hand lie there listlessly, as though her thoughts were elsewhere — somewhere ahead of her body, and she was striving to overtake them.
Robert helped her into the hammock that swung from the post before her door to the trunk of a tree.
“Will you stay out here and wait for Mr. Pontellier?” he asked.
“I’ll stay out here. Good night.”
“Shall I get you a pillow?”
“There’s one here,” she said, feeling about, for they were in the shadow.
“It must be dirty; the children have been tumbling it about.”

“No matter.” And having found the pillow, she adjusted it beneath her head. She stretched herself out in the hammock with a deep breath of relief. She was not a fussy or over-dainty woman. She was not much given to lying in the hammock, and when she did so it was with no languid, voluptuous ease, but with a restful repose that seemed to settle into her whole body.
“Shall I stay with you till Mr. Pontellier comes?” asked Robert, seating himself on the outer edge of one of the steps and taking hold of the hammock rope which was fastened to the post.
“If you wish. Don’t swing the hammock. Will you get my white shawl, which I left on the window sill over at the house?”
“No; but I shall be presently.”
“Presently?” he laughed. “Do you know what time it is? How long are you going to stay out here?”
“I don’t know. Will you get the shawl?”
“Of course I will,” he said, rising. He went over to the house, walking along the grass. She watched his figure pass in and out of the strips of moonlight. It was past midnight. It was very quiet.
When he returned with the shawl she took it and kept it in her hand. She did not put it around her.
“Did you say I should stay till Mr. Pontellier came back?”
“I said you might if you wished to.”

He settled back and rolled a cigarette, which he smoked in silence. Neither did Mrs. Pontellier speak. No multitude of words could have been more significant than those moments of silence, or more charged with the first felt stirrings of desire.

When the voices of the bathers were heard approaching, Robert said good night. She did not answer him. He thought she was asleep. Again she watched his figure pass in and out of the strips of moonlight as he walked away.

chapters.title: Chapter 11
paragraphs: “What are you doing out here, Edna? I thought I should find you in bed,” said her husband, when he discovered her lying there. He had walked up with Madame Lebrun and left her at the house. His wife did not reply.
“Are you asleep?” he asked, bending down close to look at her.
“No.” Her eyes gleamed bright and intense, with no sleepy shadows, as they looked into his.
“Do you know it is past one o’clock? Come on,” and he mounted the steps and went into their room.
“Edna!” called Mr. Pontellier from within, after a few moments had gone by.
“Don’t wait for me,” she answered. He thrust his head through the door.
“You will take cold out there,” he said, irritably. “What folly is this? Why don’t you come in?”
“It isn’t cold; I have my shawl.”
“The mosquitoes will devour you.”
“There are no mosquitoes.”

She heard him moving about the room; every sound indicating impatience and irritation. Another time she would have gone in at his request. She would, through habit, have yielded to his desire; not with any sense of submission or obedience to his compelling wishes, but unthinkingly, as we walk, move, sit, stand, go through the daily round of the life which has been portioned out to us.
“Edna, dear, are you not coming in soon?” he asked again, this time fondly, with a note of entreaty.
“No; I am going to stay out here.”
“This is more than folly,” he blurted out. “I can’t permit you to stay out there all night. You must come in the house at once.”

With a small writhing motion she settled herself more firmly in the hammock. She felt her will blaze up, stubborn and resistant. She could not at that moment have done other than denied and resisted. She wondered if her husband had ever spoken to her like that before, and if she had submitted to his command. Of course she had; she remembered that she had. But she could not understand why or how she should have yielded, feeling as she then did.
“Léonce, go to bed,” she said. “I mean to stay out here. I don’t wish to go in, and I don’t intend to. Don’t speak to me like that again; I shall not answer you.”

Mr. Pontellier had prepared for bed, but he slipped on an extra garment. He opened a bottle of wine from his small private supply in the buffet. He drank a glass, went out on the gallery, and offered a glass to his wife. She did not wish any. He drew up the rocker, hoisted his slippered feet on the rail, and began to smoke a cigar. He smoked two cigars; then he went inside and drank another glass of wine. Mrs. Pontellier again declined to accept a glass when it was offered. Mr. Pontellier once more settled himself with elevated feet and, after a reasonable interval, smoked some more cigars.

Edna began to feel like one who awakens gradually out of a dream — a delicious, grotesque, impossible dream — to feel again the realities pressing into her soul. The physical need for sleep began to overtake her; the exuberance which had sustained and exalted her spirit left her helpless and yielding to the conditions which crowded in on her.

The stillest hour of the night had come, the hour before dawn, when the world seems to hold its breath. The moon hung low, and had turned from silver to copper in the sleeping sky. The old owl no longer hooted, and the water oaks had ceased to moan as they bent their heads.
Edna arose, cramped from lying so long and still in the hammock. She tottered up the steps, clutching feebly at the post before passing into the house.
“Are you coming in, Léonce?” she asked, turning her face toward her husband.
“Yes, dear,” he answered, with a glance following a misty puff of smoke. “Just as soon as I have finished my cigar.”

chapters.title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: She slept but a few hours. They were troubled and feverish hours, disturbed with dreams that were intangible, that eluded her, leaving only an impression upon her half-awakened senses of something unattainable. She was up and dressed in the cool of the early morning. The air was invigorating and steadied her faculties somewhat. She was not seeking refreshment or help from any source, however, either external or from within. She was blindly following whatever impulse moved her, as if she had placed herself in alien hands for direction, and freed her soul of responsibility.

Most of the people at that early hour were still in bed and asleep. A few, who intended to go over to the Chêniere for mass, were moving about. The lovers, who had laid their plans the night before, were already strolling toward the wharf. The woman in black, with her Sunday prayer-book, velvet and gold-clasped, and her Sunday silver beads, was following them at no great distance. Old Monsieur Farival was up, and was more than half inclined to do anything that suggested itself. He put on his big straw hat, and taking his umbrella from the stand in the hall, followed the woman in black, never overtaking her.
The little black girl who worked Madame Lebrun’s sewing machine was sweeping the galleries with long, absent-minded strokes of the broom. Edna sent her up into the house to wake Robert.
“Tell him I am going to the Chêniere. The boat is ready; tell him to hurry.”

He had soon joined her. She had never sent for him before. She had never asked for him. She had never seemed to want him before. She did not appear conscious that she had done anything unusual in commanding his presence. He was apparently equally unconscious of anything extraordinary in the situation. But his face was suffused with a quiet glow when he met her.

They went together to the kitchen to drink coffee. There was no time for any ceremony. They stood outside the window and the cook passed them their coffee and a roll, which they drank and ate from the window sill. Edna said it tasted good.
She had not thought of coffee or of anything. He told her he had often noticed that she lacked forethought.

“Wasn’t it enough to think of going to the Chêniere and waking you up?” she laughed. “Do I have to think of everything? — as Léonce says when he’s in a bad humor. I don’t blame him; he’d never be in a bad humor if it weren’t for me.”

They took a shortcut across the sands. At a distance they could see the curious procession moving toward the wharf — the lovers, shoulder to shoulder, creeping; the woman in black, gaining steadily upon them; old Monsieur Farival, losing ground inch by inch, and a young barefooted Spanish girl, with a red kerchief on her head and a basket on her arm, bringing up the rear.

Robert knew the girl, and he talked to her a little in the boat. No one present understood what they said. Her name was Mariequita. She had a round, sly, piquant face and pretty black eyes. Her hands were small, and she kept them folded over the handle of her basket. Her feet were broad and coarse. She did not strive to hide them. Edna looked at her feet, and noticed the sand and slime between her brown toes.

Beaudelet grumbled because Mariequita was there, taking up so much room. In reality he was annoyed at having old Monsieur Farival along, who considered himself the better sailor of the two. But he would not quarrel with so old a man, so he quarreled with Mariequita. The girl was apologetic at one moment, appealing to Robert. She was saucy the next, moving her head up and down, making eyes at Robert and faces at Beaudelet.

The lovers were all alone. They saw nothing, they heard nothing. The woman in black was counting her beads for the third time. Old Monsieur Farival talked incessantly of what he knew about handling a boat, and of what Beaudelet did not know on the same subject.
Edna liked it all. She looked Mariequita up and down, from her rough brown toes to her pretty black eyes, and back again.
“Why does she look at me like that?” inquired the girl of Robert.
“Maybe she thinks you are pretty. Shall I ask her?”
“No. Is she your sweetheart?”
“She’s a married lady, and has two children.”
“Oh! well! Francisco ran away with Sylvano’s wife, who had four children. They took all his money and one of the children and stole his boat.”
“Does she understand?”
“Are those two married over there — leaning on each other?”
“Of course not,” laughed Robert.
“Of course not,” echoed Mariequita, with a serious, confirmatory bob of the head.

The sun was high up and beginning to bite. The swift breeze seemed to Edna to drive the sting of it into the pores of her face and hands. Robert held his umbrella over her. As they went cutting sideways through the water, the sails bellied taut, with the wind filling and overflowing them. Old Monsieur Farival laughed sardonically at something as he looked at the sails, and Beaudelet swore at the old man under his breath.

Sailing across the bay to the Chêniere Caminada, Edna felt as if she were being borne away from some anchorage which had held her fast, whose chains had been loosening — had snapped the night before when the mystic spirit was abroad — leaving her free to drift wherever she chose to set her sails. Robert spoke to her constantly; he no longer noticed Mariequita. The girl had shrimps in her bamboo basket, covered with Spanish moss. She beat the moss down impatiently, and muttered to herself sullenly.
“Let us go to Grande Terre tomorrow?” said Robert in a low voice.
“What shall we do there?”
“Climb up the hill to the old fort and look at the little wriggling gold snakes, and watch the lizards sun themselves.”

She gazed away toward Grande Terre and thought she would like to be alone there with Robert, in the sun, listening to the ocean’s roar and watching the slimy lizards writhe in and out among the ruins of the old fort.
“And the next day or the next we can sail to the Bayou Brulow,” he went on.
“What shall we do there?”
“Anything — cast bait for fish.”
“No; we’ll go back to Grande Terre. Let the fish alone.”
“We’ll go wherever you like,” he said. “I’ll have Tonie come over and help me patch and trim my boat. We shall not need Beaudelet nor anyone. Are you afraid of the pirogue?”

“Then I’ll take you some night in the pirogue when the moon shines. Maybe your Gulf spirit will whisper to you in which of these islands the treasures are hidden — direct you to the very spot, perhaps.”

“And in a day we should be rich!” she laughed. “I’d give it all to you, the pirate gold and every bit of treasure we could dig up. I think you would know how to spend it. Pirate gold isn’t a thing to be hoarded or put to use. It is something to squander and throw to the four winds, for the fun of seeing the golden specks fly.”
“We’d share it, and scatter it together,” he said. His face flushed.
They all went together up to the quaint little Gothic church of Our Lady of Lourdes, gleaming all brown and yellow with paint in the sun’s glare.
Only Beaudelet remained behind, tinkering at his boat, and Mariequita walked away with her basket of shrimps, casting a look of childish ill humor and reproach at Robert from the corner of her eye.

chapters.title: Chapter 13
paragraphs: A feeling of oppression and drowsiness overcame Edna during the service. Her head began to ache, and the lights on the altar swayed before her eyes. Another time she might have made an effort to regain her composure; but her one thought was to escape the stifling atmosphere of the church and reach the open air. She arose, climbing over Robert’s feet with a murmured apology. Old Monsieur Farival, flustered and curious, stood up, but seeing that Robert had followed Mrs. Pontellier, he sank back into his seat. He whispered an anxious question to the woman in black, who did not notice him or reply, but kept her eyes fastened on the pages of her velvet prayer-book.

“I felt giddy and almost overcome,” Edna said, lifting her hands instinctively to her head and pushing her straw hat up from her forehead. “I couldn’t have stayed through the service.” They were outside in the shadow of the church. Robert was full of concern.

“It was foolish to have thought of going in the first place, let alone staying. Come over to Madame Antoine’s; you can rest there.” He took her arm and led her away, looking anxiously and continuously down into her face.

How still it was, with only the voice of the sea whispering through the reeds that grew in the saltwater pools! The long line of little gray, weather-beaten houses nestled peacefully among the orange trees. It must always have been God’s day on that low, drowsy island, Edna thought. They stopped to ask for water, leaning over a jagged fence made of sea-drift.
