A youth — a mild-faced Acadian — was drawing water from the cistern, which was nothing more than a rusty buoy with an opening on one side, sunk in the ground. The water he handed them in a tin pail was not cold, but it was cool to her heated face, and it greatly refreshed her.

Madame Antoine’s cottage was at the far end of the village. She welcomed them with all the natural hospitality, as she would have opened her door to let the sunlight in. She was fat and walked heavily and clumsily across the floor. She could speak no English, but when Robert explained that the lady who accompanied him was ill and wished to rest, she was all eagerness to make Edna comfortable.

The whole place was immaculately clean, and the big four-posted bed, snow-white, invited one to repose. It stood in a small side room that looked out across a narrow grass plot toward the shed, where a disabled boat lay keel upward.

Madame Antoine had not gone to mass. Her son Tonie had, but she supposed he would soon be back, and she invited Robert to sit and wait for him. But he went and sat outside the door and smoked. Madame Antoine busied herself in the large front room preparing dinner. She was boiling mullets over a few red coals in the huge fireplace.

Edna, left alone in the little side room, loosened her clothes, removing the greater part of them. She bathed her face, her neck and arms in the basin that stood between the windows. She took off her shoes and stockings and stretched herself in the very center of the high, white bed. How luxurious it felt to rest thus in a strange, quaint bed, with its sweet country odor of laurel lingering about the sheets and mattress! She stretched her strong limbs that ached a little. She ran her fingers through her loosened hair for a while. She looked at her round arms as she held them straight up and rubbed them one after the other, observing closely, as if for the first time, the fine, firm quality and texture of her flesh. She clasped her hands above her head, and it was thus she fell asleep.

She slept lightly at first, half awake and drowsily attentive to the things about her. She could hear Madame Antoine’s heavy, scraping tread as she walked back and forth on the sanded floor. Some chickens were clucking outside the windows, scratching for bits of gravel in the grass. Later she half heard the voices of Robert and Tonie talking under the shed. She did not stir. Even her eyelids rested numb and heavily over her sleepy eyes. The voices went on — Tonie’s slow, Acadian drawl, Robert’s quick, soft, smooth French. She understood French imperfectly unless directly addressed, and the voices were only part of the other drowsy, muffled sounds lulling her senses.

When Edna awoke it was with the conviction that she had slept long and soundly. The voices were hushed under the shed. Madame Antoine’s step was no longer to be heard in the adjoining room. Even the chickens had gone elsewhere to scratch and cluck. The mosquito bar was drawn over her; the old woman had come in while she slept and let down the bar. Edna arose quietly from the bed, and looking between the curtains of the window, she saw by the slanting rays of the sun that the afternoon was far advanced. Robert was out there under the shed, reclining in the shade against the sloping keel of the overturned boat. He was reading from a book. Tonie was no longer with him. She wondered what had become of the rest of the party. She peeped out at him two or three times as she stood washing herself in the little basin between the windows.

Madame Antoine had laid some coarse, clean towels upon a chair, and had placed a box of face powder within easy reach. Edna dusted the powder upon her nose and cheeks as she looked at herself closely in the small distorted mirror which hung on the wall above the basin. Her eyes were bright and wide awake and her face glowed.

When she had finished dressing she walked into the adjoining room. She was very hungry. No one was there. But there was a cloth spread upon the table that stood against the wall, and a cover was laid for one, with a crusty brown loaf and a bottle of wine beside the plate. Edna bit a piece from the brown loaf, tearing it with her strong, white teeth. She poured some of the wine into the glass and drank it down. Then she went softly outdoors, and plucking an orange from the low-hanging bough of a tree, threw it at Robert, who did not know she was awake and up.
A light broke over his whole face when he saw her and joined her under the orange tree.

“How many years have I slept?” she inquired. “The whole island seems changed. A new race of beings must have sprung up, leaving only you and me as past relics. How many ages ago did Madame Antoine and Tonie die? And when did our people from Grand Isle disappear from the earth?”
He familiarly adjusted a ruffle upon her shoulder.

“You have slept precisely one hundred years. I was left here to guard your slumbers; and for one hundred years I have been out under the shed reading a book. The only evil I couldn’t prevent was a broiled fowl drying up.”
“If it has turned to stone, still will I eat it,” said Edna, moving with him into the house. “But really, what has become of Monsieur Farival and the others?”
“Gone hours ago. When they found that you were sleeping they thought it best not to wake you. Besides, I wouldn’t have let them. What was I here for?”
“I wonder if Léonce will be worried!” she speculated, as she seated herself at table.
“Of course not; he knows you are with me,” Robert replied, as he busied himself among sundry pans and covered dishes which had been left standing on the hearth.
“Where are Madame Antoine and her son?” asked Edna.
“Gone to Vespers, and to visit some friends, I believe. I am to take you back in Tonie’s boat whenever you are ready to go.”

He stirred the smoldering ashes till the broiled fowl began to sizzle afresh. He served her with a fine little repast, dripping the coffee anew and sharing it with her. Madame Antoine had cooked little else than the mullets, but while Edna slept Robert had foraged the island. He was childishly pleased to discover her appetite, and to see how relishingly she ate the food he had procured for her.
“Shall we go right away?” she asked, after draining her glass and brushing together the crumbs of the crusty loaf.
“The sun isn’t as low as it will be in two hours,” he answered.
“The sun will be gone in two hours.”
“Well, let it go; who cares!”

They waited a good while under the orange trees, till Madame Antoine came back, panting and waddling, with a thousand apologies to explain her absence. Tonie did not dare to return. He was shy and would not willingly face any woman except his mother.

It was very pleasant to stay there under the orange trees, while the sun dipped lower and lower, turning the western sky to flaming copper and gold. The shadows lengthened and crept out like stealthy, grotesque monsters across the grass.
Edna and Robert both sat upon the ground — that is, he lay upon the ground beside her, occasionally picking at the hem of her muslin gown.
Madame Antoine seated her fat body, broad and squat, upon a bench beside the door. She had been talking all the afternoon, and had wound herself up to the storytelling pitch.

And what stories she told them! Twice in her life she had left the Chêniere Caminada, and then for the briefest span. All her years she had squatted and waddled there upon the island, gathering legends of the Baratarians and the sea. The night came on, with the moon to lighten it. Edna could hear the whispering voices of dead men and the clink of muffled gold.
When she and Robert stepped into Tonie’s boat, with the red lateen sail, misty spirit forms were prowling in the shadows and among the reeds, and upon the water were phantom ships, speeding to cover.

chapters.title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: The youngest boy, Etienne, had been very naughty, Madame Ratignolle said, as she delivered him into the hands of his mother. He had been unwilling to go to bed and had made a scene; whereupon she had taken charge of him and pacified him as well as she could. Raoul had been in bed and asleep for two hours.

The boy was in his long white nightgown, which kept tripping him up as Madame Ratignolle led him along by the hand. With his other chubby fist he rubbed his eyes, which were heavy with sleep and ill humor. Edna took him in her arms, and seating herself in the rocker, began to coddle and caress him, calling him all manner of tender names, soothing him to sleep.
It was not more than nine o’clock. No one had yet gone to bed but the children.

Léonce had been very uneasy at first, Madame Ratignolle said, and had wanted to set out at once for the Chêniere. But Monsieur Farival had assured him that his wife was only overcome with sleep and fatigue, that Tonie would bring her safely back later in the day; and he had thus been dissuaded from crossing the bay. He had gone over to Klein’s, looking up some cotton broker whom he wished to see about securities, stocks, bonds, or something of the sort — Madame Ratignolle did not remember exactly what. He said he would not remain away late. She herself was suffering from heat and oppression, she said. She carried a bottle of salts and a large fan. She would not consent to remain with Edna, for Monsieur Ratignolle was alone, and he detested above all things to be left alone.

When Etienne had fallen asleep Edna carried him into the back room, and Robert went and lifted the mosquito bar so that she might lay the child comfortably in his bed. The quadroon had vanished. When they came out of the cottage Robert bade Edna good night.
“Do you know we have been together the whole livelong day, Robert — since early this morning?” she said at parting.
“All but the hundred years when you were sleeping. Good night.”
He pressed her hand and went away in the direction of the beach. He did not join any of the others, but walked alone toward the Gulf.

Edna stayed outside, waiting for her husband to return. She had no desire to sleep or retire; nor did she feel like going over to sit with the Ratignolles, or to join Madame Lebrun and the group whose animated voices reached her as they sat in conversation before the house. She let her mind wander back over her stay at Grand Isle; and she tried to discover wherein this summer had been different from any and every other summer of her life. She could only realize that she herself — her present self — was in some way different from the other self. That she was seeing with different eyes and making the acquaintance of new conditions in herself that colored and changed her environment, she did not yet suspect.

She wondered why Robert had gone away and left her. It did not occur to her to think he might have grown tired of being with her the livelong day. She was not tired, and she felt that he was not. She regretted that he had gone. It was so much more natural to have him stay, when he was not absolutely required to leave.
As Edna waited for her husband she sang low a little song that Robert had sung as they crossed the bay. It began with “Ah! si tu savais,” and every verse ended with “si tu savais.”
Robert’s voice was not pretentious. It was musical and true. The voice, the notes, the whole refrain haunted her memory.

chapters.title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: When Edna entered the dining room one evening, a little late as was her habit, an unusually animated conversation was underway. Several people were talking at once, and Victor’s voice was dominating even his mother’s. Edna had returned late from her swim, had dressed in some haste, and her face was flushed. Her head, set off by her delicate white gown, was like some rich, rare blossom. She took her seat between old Monsieur Farival and Madame Ratignolle.

As she sat down and was about to begin her soup, which had been served when she entered, several people told her simultaneously that Robert was going to Mexico. She put down her spoon and looked around, bewildered. He had been with her all morning, reading to her, and had never mentioned any such place as Mexico. She hadn’t seen him that afternoon; she had heard someone say he was upstairs with his mother. She had thought nothing of it, though she was surprised when he didn’t join her later, when she went down to the beach.

She looked across at him where he sat beside Madame Lebrun, who was presiding. Edna’s face was a blank picture of bewilderment, which she never thought to conceal. He raised his eyebrows with the pretense of a smile as he met her glance. He looked embarrassed and ill at ease. “When is he going?” she asked of everyone in general, as if Robert weren’t there to answer for himself.
“Tonight!” “This very evening!” “Did you ever!” “What’s gotten into him!” — these were some of the replies she received, uttered simultaneously in French and English.
“Impossible!” she exclaimed. “How can a person set off from Grand Isle to Mexico at a moment’s notice, as if he were walking over to Klein’s or down to the beach?”

“I’ve been saying all along I was going to Mexico; I’ve been saying so for years!” cried Robert, in an excited and irritable tone, with the air of a man defending himself against a swarm of stinging insects.
Madame Lebrun knocked on the table with her knife handle.

“Please let Robert explain why he is going, and why he is going tonight,” she called out. “Really, this table is becoming more like bedlam every day, with everyone talking at once. Sometimes — I hope God will forgive me — but positively, sometimes I wish Victor would lose the power of speech.”
Victor laughed sardonically as he thanked his mother for this holy wish, the benefit of which escaped him, except that it might give her more room to talk herself.

Monsieur Farival thought Victor should have been taken out to sea in his earliest years and drowned. Victor thought the logic of this more properly applied to elderly people who had earned a claim on being universally insufferable. Madame Lebrun grew a little hysterical; Robert called his brother some sharp, hard names.

“There’s not much to explain, mother,” he said; though he explained it all the same — looking mostly at Edna — that he could only meet the gentleman he intended to join at Vera Cruz by taking a particular steamer that left New Orleans on a particular day; that Beaudelet was going out with his cargo of vegetables that night, which gave him the chance to reach the city and make his vessel in time.
“But when did you make up your mind to all this?” demanded Monsieur Farival.
“This afternoon,” returned Robert, with a shade of annoyance.
“At what time this afternoon?” persisted the old gentleman, with nagging determination, as if cross-examining a criminal in a court of justice.
“At four o’clock this afternoon, Monsieur Farival,” Robert replied, in a high voice and with the air of some gentleman on a stage.
She had forced herself to eat most of her soup, and now she was picking at the flaky bits of a court-bouillon with her fork.

The lovers were taking advantage of the general conversation about Mexico to whisper to each other things of interest to no one but themselves. The woman in black had once received from Mexico a pair of prayer beads of unusual workmanship with a very special indulgence attached to them, but she had never been able to find out whether the indulgence extended beyond the Mexican border. Father Fochel of the Cathedral had tried to explain it but had not done so to her satisfaction. She begged Robert to look into it if he could, and discover whether she was entitled to the indulgence accompanying the remarkably curious Mexican prayer beads.

Madame Ratignolle hoped Robert would be very careful in his dealings with the Mexicans, whom she considered treacherous, unscrupulous, and revengeful. She trusted she did them no injustice in condemning them as a race. She had personally known only one Mexican — a man who made and sold excellent tamales and whom she would have trusted completely, so soft-spoken was he. One day he was arrested for stabbing his wife. She never found out whether he had been hanged.

Victor had become boisterous and was trying to tell an anecdote about a Mexican girl who had served chocolate one winter in a restaurant on Dauphine Street. No one would listen to him except old Monsieur Farival, who went into convulsions over the story.
Edna wondered if they had all gone mad, to be talking and clamoring at that rate. She herself could think of nothing to say about Mexico or the Mexicans.
“At what time do you leave?” she asked Robert.
“At ten,” he said. “Beaudelet wants to wait for the moon.”
“Are you all ready to go?”
“Quite ready. I’ll only take a bag and pack my trunk in the city.”
He turned to answer something his mother asked him, and Edna, having finished her black coffee, left the table.

She went directly to her room. The little cottage was close and stuffy after the open air. But she didn’t mind; there seemed to be a hundred things demanding her attention indoors. She began to set the dressing table in order, grumbling at the quadroon’s negligence — that woman was in the next room putting the children to bed. She gathered stray garments hanging on the backs of chairs and put each in its proper place in closet or bureau. She changed into a more comfortable, looser wrapper. She rearranged her hair, combing and brushing it with unusual energy. Then she went in and helped the quadroon get the boys to bed.

They were very playful and disinclined to settle — ready to do anything but lie quiet and sleep. Edna sent the quadroon off to her supper and told her not to come back. Then she sat and told the children a story. Instead of soothing them it excited them and added to their wakefulness. She left them in heated argument, speculating about how the tale would end — a conclusion their mother promised to provide the following night.

A little black girl came to say that Madame Lebrun would like Mrs. Pontellier to come and sit with them at the main house until Mr. Robert went away. Edna sent back word that she had already undressed and was not feeling quite well, but perhaps she would come later. She started to dress again, got as far as removing her peignoir. But changing her mind she put it back on and went outside and sat down before her door. She was overheated and irritable, and fanned herself energetically for a while. Madame Ratignolle came down to find out what the matter was.

“All that noise and confusion at the table must have upset me,” replied Edna, “and moreover, I hate shocks and surprises. The idea of Robert starting off in such a ridiculously sudden and dramatic way! As if it were a matter of life and death! Never saying a word about it all morning when he was with me.”

“Yes,” agreed Madame Ratignolle. “I think it was showing us all — you especially — very little consideration. It wouldn’t have surprised me from the others; those Lebruns are all given to heroics. But I must say I never would have expected such a thing from Robert. Are you not coming down? Come, dear; it doesn’t look friendly.”
“No,” said Edna, a little sullenly. “I can’t be bothered dressing again; I don’t feel like it.”
“You needn’t dress; you look fine; just fasten a belt around your waist. Just look at me!”
“No,” persisted Edna; “but you go on. Madame Lebrun might take offense if we both stayed away.”
Madame Ratignolle kissed Edna good night and went away, being in truth rather eager to join in the animated conversation about Mexico and the Mexicans that was still in progress.
Somewhat later Robert came up, carrying his bag.
“Aren’t you feeling well?” he asked.
“Oh, well enough. Are you going right away?”

He lit a match and looked at his watch. “In twenty minutes,” he said. The sudden brief flare of the match emphasized the darkness for a moment. He sat down on a small stool the children had left out on the porch.
“Get a chair,” said Edna.
“This will do,” he replied. He put on his soft hat and nervously took it off again, and wiping his face with his handkerchief, complained of the heat.
“Take the fan,” said Edna, offering it to him.
“Oh, no! Thank you. It does no good; you have to stop fanning eventually, and feel all the worse for it afterward.”
“That’s one of the ridiculous things men always say. I’ve never heard one say anything different about fanning. How long will you be gone?”
“Forever, perhaps. I don’t know. It depends on a good many things.”
“Well, in case it shouldn’t be forever, how long will it be?”

“This seems to me quite preposterous and uncalled for. I don’t like it. I don’t understand why you kept it from me all morning, not saying a word.” He remained silent, offering no defense. He only said, after a moment:
“Don’t let us part in bad feeling. I’ve never known you to be out of patience with me before.”

“I don’t want to part in bad feeling,” she said. “But can’t you understand? I’ve grown used to seeing you, to having you with me every day, and this feels unfriendly — even unkind. You don’t even offer an explanation. Why, I was planning things — thinking how pleasant it would be to see you in the city this winter.”

“So was I,” he blurted. “Perhaps that’s the —” He stood up suddenly and held out his hand. “Goodbye, my dear Mrs. Pontellier; goodbye. You won’t — I hope you won’t completely forget me.” She clung to his hand, trying to keep him from going.
“Write to me when you get there, won’t you, Robert?” she entreated.
“I will, thank you. Goodbye.”
How unlike Robert! The merest acquaintance would have said something warmer than “I will, thank you; goodbye” to such a request.

He had evidently already taken leave of the people at the main house, for he went down the steps and joined Beaudelet, who was waiting with an oar across his shoulder. They walked away into the darkness. She could hear only Beaudelet’s voice; Robert had apparently not even spoken a word of greeting to his companion.

Edna bit her handkerchief convulsively, struggling to hold back and to hide — even from herself, as she would have hidden from another — the emotion that was troubling, tearing at her. Her eyes were brimming with tears.

For the first time she recognized the symptoms of infatuation which she had first felt, faintly, as a child, as a girl in her early teens, and later as a young woman. The recognition did not diminish the reality or the poignancy of the revelation by any suggestion of instability or promise that it would pass. The past meant nothing to her; it offered no lesson she was willing to receive. The future was a mystery she never attempted to penetrate. The present alone was real; it was hers, and it tortured her then with the biting knowledge that she had lost what she had held, that she had been denied what her newly awakened, impassioned being demanded.

chapters.title: Chapter 16
paragraphs: “Do you miss your friend very much?” asked Mademoiselle Reisz one morning, coming up behind Edna, who had just left her cottage on her way to the beach. She had spent a great deal of time in the water since she had finally learned to swim. As their stay at Grand Isle drew near its end, she felt she could never have too much of the one diversion that gave her any real pleasure. When Mademoiselle Reisz came up behind her and spoke, the woman seemed to echo the thought — or, better, the feeling — that was constantly with Edna.

Robert’s going had somehow drained the brightness, the color, the meaning out of everything. The outward conditions of her life were unchanged, but her whole existence was dulled, like a faded garment that no longer seems worth putting on. She looked for him everywhere — in others whom she got to talk about him. She went up mornings to Madame Lebrun’s room, braving the clatter of the old sewing machine. She sat there and chatted at intervals as Robert used to. She looked around at the pictures and photographs on the wall, and found in a corner an old family album, which she examined with the keenest interest, asking Madame Lebrun about the many faces she encountered between its pages.

There was a picture of Madame Lebrun with Robert as a baby on her lap — a round-faced infant with a fist in his mouth. In the baby’s eyes alone you could see the man. There he was again in a kilt at five, wearing long curls and holding a whip in his hand. That made Edna laugh; she laughed too at the portrait of him in his first long trousers. Another interested her — taken when he left for college, looking thin and long-faced, his eyes full of fire, ambition, and great intentions. But there was no recent picture, nothing that suggested the Robert who had gone away five days ago, leaving a void and a wilderness behind him.

“Oh, Robert stopped having his photograph taken when he had to pay for it himself! He found better uses for his money, he says,” explained Madame Lebrun. She had a letter from him, written before he left New Orleans. Edna asked to see it, and Madame Lebrun told her to look for it on the table or the dresser, or perhaps the mantelpiece.

The letter was on the bookshelf. Everything about it fascinated Edna — the envelope, its size and shape, the postmark, the handwriting. She examined every detail of the outside before opening it. There were only a few lines, saying he would leave the city that afternoon, that he had packed his trunk in good shape, that he was well, and sending his love and asking to be remembered affectionately to all. There was no special message to Edna, only a postscript saying that if Mrs. Pontellier wished to finish the book he had been reading to her, his mother would find it in his room, on the table among his other books. Edna felt a pang of jealousy that he had written to his mother rather than to her.
Everyone seemed to take it for granted that she missed him. Even her husband, when he came down the Saturday after Robert’s departure, expressed regret that he had gone.
“How do you get on without him, Edna?” he asked.

“It’s very dull without him,” she admitted. Mr. Pontellier had seen Robert in the city, and Edna asked him a dozen questions or more. Where had they met? On Carondelet Street, in the morning. They had gone in for a drink and a cigar together. What had they talked about? Chiefly about his prospects in Mexico, which Mr. Pontellier found encouraging. How did he look? How did he seem — serious, or cheerful, or how? Quite cheerful, and entirely taken up with his trip, which Mr. Pontellier thought perfectly natural in a young man about to seek fortune and adventure in a strange country.

Edna tapped her foot impatiently, and wondered why the children kept playing in the sun when they could be under the trees. She went down and led them out of the sun, scolding the quadroon for not being more attentive.

It did not strike her as the least bit strange that she should be steering the conversation toward Robert and getting her husband to speak of him. The feeling she had for Robert in no way resembled what she felt or had ever felt or expected to feel for her husband. All her life she had been accustomed to harbor thoughts and emotions that never found expression. They had never taken the form of struggles. They belonged to her alone, and she believed she had the right to them, that they concerned no one but herself. Edna had once told Madame Ratignolle that she would never sacrifice herself for her children or for anyone. A rather heated argument had followed; the two women seemed unable to understand each other or to be speaking the same language. Edna tried to appease her friend, to explain.

“I would give up the unessential; I would give my money, I would give my life for my children; but I wouldn’t give myself. I can’t make it more clear; it’s only something I’m beginning to understand, that is revealing itself to me.”

“I don’t know what you would call the essential, or what you mean by the unessential,” said Madame Ratignolle cheerfully; “but a woman who would give her life for her children could do no more than that — your Bible says so. I’m sure I couldn’t do more than that.”
“Oh, yes you could!” laughed Edna.
She was not surprised at Mademoiselle Reisz’s question the morning that lady, following her to the beach, tapped her on the shoulder and asked if she didn’t greatly miss her young friend.
“Oh, good morning, Mademoiselle; is it you? Why, of course I miss Robert. Are you coming down to swim?”
“Why should I go down to swim at the very end of the season when I haven’t been in the water all summer?” replied the woman, disagreeably.

“I beg your pardon,” offered Edna, in some embarrassment, for she should have remembered that Mademoiselle Reisz’s avoidance of the water had been the subject of considerable amusement. Some thought it was on account of her false hair, or the fear of getting her violets wet; others attributed it to the natural aversion to water sometimes associated with the artistic temperament. Mademoiselle offered Edna some chocolates from a paper bag she took from her pocket, by way of showing she bore no ill feeling. She habitually ate chocolates for their sustaining properties; they contained a great deal of nourishment in a small space, she said. They saved her from starvation, as Madame Lebrun’s table was utterly impossible, and no one but a woman of Madame Lebrun’s impudence could think of offering such food to people and charging for it.
“She must feel very lonely without her son,” said Edna, wanting to change the subject. “Her favorite son, too. It must have been hard to let him go.”
Mademoiselle laughed, not kindly.

“Her favorite son! Oh dear! Who has been telling you that? Aline Lebrun lives for Victor, and for Victor alone. She has spoiled him into the worthless creature he is. She worships him and the ground he walks on. Robert is useful enough in his way — giving up all the money he can earn to the family and keeping the barest pittance for himself. Favorite son, indeed! I miss the poor fellow myself, my dear. I liked to see him and hear him about the place — the only Lebrun worth anything. He comes to see me often in the city. I like to play for him. That Victor! Hanging would be too good for him. It’s a wonder Robert hasn’t beaten him to death long ago.”
“I thought he had great patience with his brother,” offered Edna, glad to be talking about Robert, regardless of what was said.

“Oh, he gave him a thorough thrashing a year or two ago,” said Mademoiselle. “It was over a Spanish girl, whom Victor believed he had some sort of claim on. He ran into Robert one day talking to the girl, or walking with her, or swimming with her, or carrying her basket — I don’t remember what — and he became so insulting and abusive that Robert gave him a beating right then and there that kept him comparatively in order for some time. It’s about time he was getting another.”
“Was her name Mariequita?” asked Edna.
“Mariequita — yes, that was it; Mariequita. I had forgotten. Oh, she’s a sly one, and a bad one, that Mariequita!”

Edna looked at Mademoiselle Reisz and wondered how she had managed to listen to her venom for so long. For some reason she felt depressed, almost unhappy. She had not intended to go into the water; but she put on her bathing suit and left Mademoiselle sitting alone under the shade of the children’s tent. The water was growing cooler as the season advanced. Edna plunged in and swam about with an abandon that thrilled and invigorated her. She stayed in a long time, half hoping Mademoiselle would not wait for her.

But Mademoiselle waited. She was very pleasant on the walk back, and talked enthusiastically about Edna’s appearance in her bathing suit. She talked about music. She hoped Edna would come to see her in the city, and wrote her address with a pencil stub on a piece of card from her pocket.
“When do you leave?” asked Edna.
“Next Monday; and you?”
“The following week,” answered Edna, adding, “It has been a pleasant summer, hasn’t it, Mademoiselle?”
“Well,” agreed Mademoiselle Reisz, with a shrug, “rather pleasant, if it hadn’t been for the mosquitoes and the Farival twins.”

chapters.title: Chapter 17
paragraphs: The Pontelliers owned a very fine house on Esplanade Street in New Orleans. It was a large, double cottage with a broad front veranda whose round, fluted columns supported the sloping roof. The house was painted a dazzling white; the outside shutters, or jalousies, were green. The yard, kept scrupulously neat, had flowers and plants of every description that flourishes in south Louisiana. Inside, the appointments were perfect in the conventional style. The softest carpets and rugs covered the floors; rich and tasteful draperies hung at doors and windows. Paintings, chosen with judgment, hung on the walls. The cut glass, the silver, the heavy damask that appeared on the table daily were the envy of many women whose husbands were less generous than Mr. Pontellier.

Mr. Pontellier was fond of walking through his house and examining its many appointments and details, checking that nothing was amiss. He greatly valued his possessions, chiefly because they were his, and derived genuine pleasure from contemplating a painting, a statuette, a fine lace curtain — no matter what — after he had bought it and placed it among his household treasures.

On Tuesday afternoons — Tuesday being Mrs. Pontellier’s reception day — there was a constant stream of callers: women who came in carriages or streetcars, or walked when the air was soft and the distance permitted. A light-skinned mulatto boy in a dress coat, carrying a small silver tray for visiting cards, admitted them. A maid in a white ruffled cap offered the callers liqueur, coffee, or chocolate, as they preferred. Mrs. Pontellier, in a handsome reception gown, received them in the drawing room all afternoon. Men sometimes called in the evenings with their wives.
This had been Mrs. Pontellier’s strict routine since her marriage, six years before. On certain evenings she and her husband attended the opera or sometimes the theater.
Mr. Pontellier left home between nine and ten in the mornings and rarely returned before half past six or seven in the evening — dinner being served at half past seven.

He and his wife sat down to dinner one Tuesday evening, a few weeks after their return from Grand Isle. They were alone. The boys were being put to bed; the patter of their bare, escaping feet could be heard now and again, along with the pursuing voice of the quadroon raised in mild protest and entreaty. Mrs. Pontellier was not wearing her usual Tuesday reception gown; she was in an ordinary house dress. Mr. Pontellier, who noticed such things, saw this as he served the soup and handed it to the waiting boy.
“Tired out, Edna? How many callers did you have?” he asked. He tasted his soup and began to season it with pepper, salt, vinegar, mustard — everything within reach.
“There were quite a few,” replied Edna, eating her soup with evident satisfaction. “I found their cards when I got home; I was out.”

“Out!” exclaimed her husband, with something like genuine consternation, setting down the vinegar cruet and looking at her through his glasses. “Why, what could have taken you out on Tuesday? What did you have to do?”
“Nothing. I simply felt like going out, and I went out.”
“Well, I hope you left some suitable excuse,” said her husband, somewhat appeased, adding a dash of cayenne to the soup.
“No, I left no excuse. I told Joe to say I was out, that was all.”

“My dear, I should think you’d understand by now that people don’t do such things; we have to observe les convenances if we ever expect to get on and keep up with the world. If you felt you had to go out this afternoon, you should have left a suitable explanation for your absence.
“This soup is really impossible; it’s strange that woman hasn’t learned yet to make a decent soup. Any lunch counter in town serves a better one. Was Mrs. Belthrop here?”
“Bring the tray with the cards, Joe. I don’t remember who was here.”
The boy went out and returned with the small silver tray covered with visiting cards. He handed it to Mrs. Pontellier.
“Give it to Mr. Pontellier,” she said.
Joe offered the tray to Mr. Pontellier and removed the soup.
Mr. Pontellier went through his wife’s callers’ names, reading some aloud with commentary.

“‘The Misses Delasidas.’ I handled a big deal in futures for their father this morning; nice girls; it’s time they were married. ‘Mrs. Belthrop.’ I tell you, Edna, you can’t afford to snub Mrs. Belthrop. Why, Belthrop could buy and sell us ten times over. His business is worth a good deal to me. You’d better write her a note. ‘Mrs. James Highcamp.’ The less you have to do with Mrs. Highcamp, the better. ‘Madame Laforce.’ Came all the way from Carrollton, poor old soul. ‘Miss Wiggs.’ ‘Mrs. Eleanor Boltons.’” He pushed the cards aside.
“Mercy!” exclaimed Edna, who had been fuming. “Why are you taking the thing so seriously and making such a fuss over it?”
“I’m not making a fuss over it. But it’s just such apparently minor things that we have to take seriously; such things count.”

The fish was scorched. Mr. Pontellier would not touch it. Edna said she didn’t mind a slightly scorched taste. The roast was not to his fancy either, and he did not like the way the vegetables were served.
“It seems to me,” he said, “we spend enough in this house to have at least one meal a day that a man can eat and retain his self-respect.”
“You used to think the cook was a treasure,” returned Edna, indifferently.

“Perhaps she was when she first came; but cooks are only human. They need managing, like any other class of employees. Suppose I didn’t supervise the clerks in my office, just let them run things their own way — they’d soon make a fine mess of me and my business.”
“Where are you going?” asked Edna, seeing that her husband had risen from the table without having eaten a morsel except a taste of the over-seasoned soup.
“I’m going to eat dinner at the club. Good night.” He went into the hall, took his hat and stick, and left the house.

She was somewhat used to such scenes. They had often made her very unhappy. On previous occasions they had left her without any desire to finish her dinner. Sometimes she had gone into the kitchen to scold the cook. Once she had gone to her room and studied the cookbook for an entire evening, finally writing out a week’s menus, which left her with the unsatisfying feeling that she had accomplished nothing worth the name.

But that evening Edna finished her dinner alone, with a deliberate calm. Her face was flushed and her eyes burned with some inner fire that lit them from within. After finishing she went to her room, having told the boy to inform any other callers that she was indisposed.

It was a large, beautiful room, rich and atmospheric in the soft, dim light the maid had turned low. She went and stood at an open window and looked down at the deep, tangled garden below. All the mystery and enchantment of the night seemed to have gathered there among the perfumes and shadowy, tortuous outlines of flowers and foliage. She was seeking herself and finding herself in just such sweet half-darkness, which suited her mood. But the voices that came to her from the darkness and the sky and the stars were not soothing. They mocked her and sounded mournful notes without promise, without even hope. She turned back into the room and began to walk its length back and forth without stopping, without resting. She carried in her hands a thin handkerchief, which she tore into ribbons, rolled into a ball, and flung away. Once she stopped and, taking off her wedding ring, flung it on the carpet. When she saw it lying there, she stamped her heel upon it, trying to crush it. But her small boot heel made not a dent, not a mark upon the little glittering circlet.
In a burst of fury she seized a glass vase from the table and flung it on the tiles of the hearth. She wanted to destroy something. The crash and clatter were what she wanted to hear.
A maid, alarmed by the sound of breaking glass, entered the room to find out what had happened.
“A vase fell on the hearth,” said Edna. “Never mind; leave it till morning.”
“Oh, you might get some of the glass in your feet, ma’am,” insisted the young woman, picking up fragments of the broken vase from the carpet. “And here’s your ring, ma’am, under the chair.”
Edna held out her hand, took the ring, and slipped it back on her finger.

chapters.title: Chapter 18
paragraphs: The next morning, as Mr. Pontellier left for his office, he asked Edna if she would meet him downtown to look at new fixtures for the library.
“I hardly think we need new fixtures, Léonce. Let’s not buy anything new—you’re far too extravagant. I don’t believe you ever think about saving.”

“The way to become rich, my dear Edna, is to make money, not to save it,” he said. He was sorry she didn’t feel like coming with him. He kissed her goodbye and told her she wasn’t looking well and should take care of herself. She was unusually pale and very quiet.

She stood on the front veranda as he left the house, absently picking a few sprays of jessamine from the trellis nearby. She breathed in their scent and tucked them into the front of her white morning gown. The boys were dragging a small express wagon along the banquette, filled with blocks and sticks, the quadroon following close behind with quick little steps, having put on an air of cheerful busyness for the occasion. A fruit vendor was calling his wares in the street.

Edna stared straight ahead with a self-absorbed expression on her face. Nothing around her held any interest. The street, the children, the fruit vendor, the flowers growing just below her eyes—all of it seemed part of a foreign world that had suddenly turned hostile.

She went back inside. She had meant to speak to the cook about her blunders the night before; but Mr. Pontellier had spared her that disagreeable task, for which she was poorly fitted. His arguments were usually persuasive with the household staff. He left home feeling certain that he and Edna would sit down that evening—and perhaps several evenings after—to a dinner deserving of the name.

Edna spent an hour or two looking over some of her old sketches. She could see their flaws clearly now; they were glaring to her eye. She tried to work a little but found she wasn’t in the mood. At last she gathered a few—the least embarrassing among them—and carried them with her when she dressed and left the house a little later. She looked handsome and distinguished in her street dress. The tan from the seashore had faded, and her forehead was smooth, white, and polished beneath her heavy yellow-brown hair. A few freckles scattered across her face, and there was a small dark mole near her lower lip and another at her temple, half hidden in her hair.

As Edna walked along the street, she was thinking of Robert. She was still under the spell of her feeling for him. She had tried to forget him, knowing it was pointless to dwell on him. But the thought of him was like an obsession, pressing itself upon her constantly. It was not any particular memory of their time together—it was his existence, his very being, that dominated her mind, fading at times as if it might dissolve into forgetting, then reviving with an intensity that filled her with an incomprehensible longing.

Edna was on her way to Madame Ratignolle’s. Their friendship, begun at Grand Isle, had only deepened, and they had seen each other often since returning to the city. The Ratignolles lived not far from Edna’s home, on the corner of a side street where Monsieur Ratignolle owned and ran a drugstore with a steady and prosperous trade. His father had been in the business before him, and Monsieur Ratignolle stood well in the community, known for his integrity and good sense. The family lived in spacious apartments above the store, with an entrance on the side beneath the porte cochère. There was something Edna found very French, very foreign, about the whole way they lived. In the large, pleasant salon that stretched across the width of the house, the Ratignolles entertained their friends every two weeks with a soirée musicale, sometimes varied by card-playing. One friend played the cello. Another brought his flute, another his violin, while some sang and a number performed at the piano with varying degrees of skill. The Ratignolles’ soirées musicales were widely known, and to be invited was considered a privilege.

Edna found her friend occupied with sorting laundry that had returned from the wash that morning. Madame Ratignolle abandoned her task the moment she saw Edna, who had been ushered in without ceremony.

“’Cité can do it just as well—it’s really her job,” she explained to Edna, who apologized for interrupting. She summoned a young Black woman and gave her instructions in French: be very careful checking the list, look particularly for a fine linen handkerchief of Monsieur Ratignolle’s that had gone missing the week before, and set aside anything that needed mending.
Then she put an arm around Edna’s waist and led her to the front of the house, to the salon, where it was cool and sweet with the scent of great roses in jars on the hearth.
Madame Ratignolle looked more beautiful than ever there at home, in a negligé that left her arms nearly bare and exposed the rich, melting curves of her white throat.

“Perhaps I’ll be able to paint your portrait one day,” Edna said with a smile as they sat down. She unrolled her sketches. “I think I should work again. I feel as if I want to be doing something. What do you think of these? Is it worth taking it up again and studying more? I might study for a while with Laidpore.”

She knew that Madame Ratignolle’s opinion on such matters would be worthless, and that she had already decided for herself—but she wanted the words of praise and encouragement that would help her put heart into the venture.
“Your talent is immense, dear!”
“Nonsense!” protested Edna, well pleased.

“Immense, I tell you,” Madame Ratignolle insisted, examining the sketches one by one, holding them close, then at arm’s length, narrowing her eyes and tilting her head. “Surely this Bavarian peasant is worth framing, and this basket of apples—I’ve never seen anything more lifelike. One might almost reach out and take one.”

Edna couldn’t help feeling something close to complacency at her friend’s praise, even knowing exactly what it was worth. She kept a few of the sketches and gave the rest to Madame Ratignolle, who valued the gift far beyond its merit and proudly showed the pictures to her husband when he came up from the store for his midday dinner.

Monsieur Ratignolle was one of those men called the salt of the earth. His cheerfulness was boundless, matched by his goodness of heart, his broad charity, and his common sense. He and his wife spoke English with an accent discernible only through its un-English emphasis and a certain deliberateness. Edna’s husband spoke English with no accent whatever. The Ratignolles understood each other perfectly. If the fusion of two human beings into one has ever been accomplished on this earth, it was surely in their union.

As Edna sat at table with them she thought, “Better a dinner of herbs”—though it did not take her long to discover that it was no dinner of herbs, but a delicious meal, simple, fine, and entirely satisfying.

Monsieur Ratignolle was delighted to see her, though he thought she looked less well than at Grand Isle and advised a tonic. He talked at length on various subjects—a little politics, city news, neighborhood gossip—with an animation and earnestness that gave exaggerated weight to every syllable. His wife listened keenly to everything he said, setting down her fork the better to hear, chiming in, taking the words from his mouth.

Edna felt depressed rather than soothed when she left them. The brief glimpse of domestic harmony she had been offered left her no regret, no longing. It was not a life that fitted her, and she could see in it only an appalling, hopeless ennui. She felt something like pity for Madame Ratignolle—pity for that colorless existence which never lifted its possessor beyond the region of blind contentment, in which no moment of anguish ever visited her soul, in which she would never taste life’s delirium. Edna vaguely wondered what she meant by “life’s delirium.” It had crossed her mind like some passing, uninvited impression.

chapters.title: Chapter 19
paragraphs: Edna couldn’t help thinking it had been very foolish, very childish, to have stamped on her wedding ring and smashed the crystal vase against the tiles. There were no more such outbursts, no more futile expedients. She began to do as she liked and to feel as she liked. She gave up her Tuesdays at home entirely and did not return the calls of those who had visited her. She made no strained effort to run her household en bonne ménagère, coming and going as her fancy suited, and lending herself, as far as she was able, to whatever caprice happened to pass through her.

Mr. Pontellier had been a courteous enough husband as long as he encountered a certain tacit submissiveness in his wife. But her new and unexpected conduct left him bewildered. It shocked him. Then her complete disregard for her duties as a wife made him angry. When Mr. Pontellier grew rude, Edna grew insolent. She had resolved never to take another step backward.
“It seems to me the height of folly for a woman at the head of a household, and the mother of children, to spend in an atelier days that would be better spent seeing to her family’s comfort.”
“I feel like painting,” answered Edna. “Though perhaps I won’t always feel like it.”

“Then for God’s sake paint! But don’t let the family go to the devil. There’s Madame Ratignolle—she keeps up her music and doesn’t let everything else fall to chaos. And she’s more of a musician than you are a painter.”
“She’s not a musician, and I’m not a painter. It isn’t on account of painting that I let things go.”
“On account of what, then?”
“Oh! I don’t know. Leave me alone—you bother me.”

It sometimes crossed Mr. Pontellier’s mind to wonder whether his wife were growing a little mentally unbalanced. He could see plainly that she was not herself. That is, he could not see that she was becoming herself and daily casting off that fictitious self which we put on like a garment to appear before the world.

Her husband left her alone as she had asked and went to his office. Edna went up to her atelier—a bright room at the top of the house. She worked with great energy and interest, without producing anything that satisfied her even slightly. For a time she had the whole household enlisted in the service of art. The boys posed for her. They found it amusing at first, but the occupation quickly lost its appeal when they realized it was not a game arranged for their entertainment. The quadroon sat for hours before Edna’s palette, patient as a statue, while the housemaid looked after the children and the drawing room went undusted. But the housemaid too served her term as a model when Edna noticed that the young woman’s back and shoulders were molded on classic lines and that her hair, freed from its cap, became an inspiration. While she worked, Edna sometimes sang low the little air, “Ah! si tu savais!”

It moved her with memories. She could hear the ripple of the water again, the flapping sail. She could see the moonlight glinting on the bay and feel the soft, gusty beat of the hot south wind. A subtle current of desire passed through her body, weakening her grip on the brushes and making her eyes burn.

There were days when she was very happy without knowing why—glad to be alive and breathing, when her whole being seemed to be one with the sunlight, the color, the fragrance, the warm luxury of some perfect Southern day. On such days she liked to wander alone into strange and unfamiliar places. She discovered many a sunny, sleepy corner that seemed made for dreaming. And she found it good to dream and to be alone and unmolested.

There were days when she was unhappy, she did not know why—when it did not seem worth while to be glad or sorry, to be alive or dead; when life appeared like a grotesque pandemonium and humanity like worms struggling blindly toward inevitable annihilation. She could not work on such a day, nor weave fancies to stir her pulses and warm her blood.

chapters.title: Chapter 20
paragraphs: It was in such a mood that Edna went in search of Mademoiselle Reisz. She hadn’t forgotten the rather disagreeable impression left by their last meeting, but she felt a strong desire to see her—above all, to listen while she played the piano. She set out early in the afternoon to find the pianist. Unfortunately she had misplaced Mademoiselle Reisz’s card, and checking the city directory she found that the woman lived on Bienville Street, some distance away. The directory was at least a year out of date, however, and when she reached the address she found it occupied by a respectable family of mulattoes who had furnished rooms to let. They had been living there six months and knew absolutely nothing of a Mademoiselle Reisz. In fact, they knew nothing of any of their neighbors—their lodgers were all people of the highest distinction, they assured Edna. She did not linger to discuss class distinctions with Madame Pouponne but hurried to a nearby grocery store, certain that Mademoiselle would have left her address with the proprietor.

He knew Mademoiselle Reisz a good deal better than he wanted to, he informed his questioner. In truth, he did not want to know her at all or anything about her—the most disagreeable and unpopular woman who had ever lived on Bienville Street. He thanked heaven she had left the neighborhood, and was equally glad he didn’t know where she had gone.

Edna’s desire to see Mademoiselle Reisz had grown tenfold now that these unexpected obstacles had arisen. She was wondering who could tell her what she needed to know when it suddenly occurred to her that Madame Lebrun would be the most likely person. She knew it was useless to ask Madame Ratignolle, who was on the most distant terms with the musician and preferred to know nothing about her. She had once been nearly as emphatic on the subject as the corner grocer.
Edna knew that Madame Lebrun had returned to the city—it was mid-November now. And she knew where the Lebruns lived, on Chartres Street.

From the outside their house looked like a prison, with iron bars before the door and lower windows. The bars were a relic of the old régime, and no one had ever thought to remove them. On the side was a high fence enclosing the garden. A gate opening onto the street was locked. Edna rang the bell at this side garden gate and stood on the banquette, waiting to be admitted.

It was Victor who opened the gate. Close on his heels was a Black woman wiping her hands on her apron. Before she even saw them, Edna heard them arguing—the woman, plainly an anomaly, claiming the right to do her duties, one of which was to answer the bell.

Victor was surprised and delighted to see Mrs. Pontellier and made no effort to conceal either. He was a dark-browed, handsome young man of nineteen, greatly resembling his mother but with ten times her impetuosity. He directed the Black woman to go at once and inform Madame Lebrun that Mrs. Pontellier wished to see her. The woman grumbled that she refused to do part of her duty when she hadn’t been permitted to do it all, and turned back to her interrupted task of weeding the garden. Whereupon Victor unleashed a volley of abuse so rapid and incoherent it was nearly incomprehensible to Edna. Whatever it was, it was effective—the woman dropped her hoe and went mumbling into the house.

Edna had no wish to go inside. It was pleasant on the side porch, with chairs, a wicker lounge, and a small table. She sat down, tired from her long walk, and began to rock gently, smoothing the folds of her silk parasol. Victor drew up a chair beside her. He immediately explained that the Black woman’s offensive conduct was entirely the result of poor training, since he had not been there to manage her. He had only come up from the island the morning before and expected to return the next day. He lived there year-round, keeping the place in order and preparing things for the summer visitors.

But a man needed occasional relaxation, he informed Mrs. Pontellier, and every now and then he drummed up a pretext to bring him to the city. My! But he’d had quite a time of it the evening before! He wouldn’t want his mother to know, and he began to whisper. He was sparkling with recollections. He couldn’t of course tell Mrs. Pontellier everything—she being a woman and not comprehending such things. But it had all begun with a girl peeping and smiling at him through the shutters as he passed. Oh! But she was a beauty! He had naturally smiled back and gone up to talk to her. Despite herself, the young man amused her. She must have let some trace of interest show, for he grew bolder, and Mrs. Pontellier might have found herself listening to a thoroughly vivid story had Madame Lebrun not appeared at that moment.

That lady was still dressed in white, as was her custom in summer. Her eyes shone with an effusive welcome. Would not Mrs. Pontellier come inside? Would she have some refreshment? Why had she not come sooner? How was dear Mr. Pontellier, and how were those sweet children? Had Mrs. Pontellier ever known such a warm November?

Victor went and reclined on the wicker lounge behind his mother’s chair, where he had a clear view of Edna’s face. He had taken her parasol from her while he talked and now lifted it and twirled it above him as he lay on his back. When Madame Lebrun complained of the dullness of coming back to the city, of seeing so few people now—even Victor, when he came up from the island for a day or two, had so much to occupy him—the young man on the lounge went through contortions of silent laughter and winked mischievously at Edna. She felt like a confederate in some crime and tried to look severe.

There had been only two letters from Robert, with little in them. Victor said it was really not worth going inside for the letters when his mother urged him to fetch them. He claimed to remember the contents and rattled them off glibly when put to the test.

One letter was from Vera Cruz, the other from Mexico City. He had met Montel, who was doing everything to help him get ahead. Financially the situation was no better than it had been in New Orleans, but the prospects were much improved. He described Mexico City—its buildings, its people, their habits, the conditions of life he found there. He sent his love to the family. He enclosed a check for his mother and hoped she would remember him affectionately to all his friends. That was the substance of both letters. Edna felt certain that had there been any message for her, she would have received it. The gloom that had settled over her when she left home began to return, and she remembered she had wanted to find Mademoiselle Reisz.

Madame Lebrun knew where Mademoiselle Reisz lived. She gave Edna the address, sorry that she would not stay and spend the rest of the afternoon, suggesting Edna visit Mademoiselle some other day. The afternoon was already well advanced.

Victor escorted her to the banquette, took her parasol, and held it over her as he walked with her to the car. He entreated her to remember that the afternoon’s disclosures were strictly confidential. She laughed and teased him a little, remembering too late that she should have been more dignified.
“How handsome Mrs. Pontellier looked!” said Madame Lebrun to her son.
“Ravishing,” he agreed. “The city air has improved her. Somehow she doesn’t seem like the same woman.”

chapters.title: Chapter 21
paragraphs: Some people claimed that the reason Mademoiselle Reisz always chose apartments up under the roof was to discourage beggars, peddlers, and callers. Her little front room had plenty of windows. They were mostly grimy, but as they were nearly always open it hardly mattered. They let in a good deal of smoke and soot but also all the light and air there was. From them you could see the crescent of the river, the masts of ships, and the great smokestacks of the Mississippi steamers. A magnificent piano crowded the apartment. In the next room she slept, and in the third and last she kept a gasoline stove on which she cooked her meals when she didn’t feel like going down to the neighboring restaurant. It was there also that she ate, keeping her things in an old buffet, dingy and battered from a hundred years of use.

When Edna knocked at Mademoiselle Reisz’s front room door and entered, she found the woman standing by the window, mending an old prunella gaiter. The little musician laughed all over when she saw Edna—her laugh was a contortion of the face and all the muscles of her body. She looked strikingly homely there in the afternoon light, still wearing the shabby lace and the artificial cluster of violets pinned to the side of her head.
“So you remembered me at last,” said Mademoiselle. “I had said to myself, ‘Ah, bah! she will never come.’”
“Did you want me to come?” asked Edna with a smile.

“I had not thought much about it,” answered Mademoiselle. They had seated themselves on a little bumpy sofa against the wall. “I am glad, however, that you came. I have water boiling back there and was just about to make coffee. You will have a cup with me. And how is la belle dame? Always handsome! always healthy! always contented!” She took Edna’s hand between her strong, wiry fingers, holding it loosely without warmth and executing a kind of double theme across the back and palm.

“Yes,” she went on; “I sometimes thought: ‘She will never come. She promised as those women in society always do, without meaning it. She will not come.’ For I really don’t believe you like me, Mrs. Pontellier.”
“I don’t know whether I like you or not,” replied Edna, gazing down at the little woman with a quizzical look.

The candor of Mrs. Pontellier’s admission greatly pleased Mademoiselle Reisz. She expressed her gratification by going at once to the gasoline stove and rewarding her guest with the promised coffee. The coffee and the biscuit accompanying it were very welcome to Edna, who had declined refreshment at Madame Lebrun’s and was now beginning to feel hungry. Mademoiselle brought in the tray, set it on a small table nearby, and sat once more on the lumpy sofa.
“I have had a letter from your friend,” she remarked, as she poured a little cream into Edna’s cup and handed it to her.
“Yes, your friend Robert. He wrote to me from Mexico City.”
“Wrote to you?” repeated Edna in amazement, stirring her coffee absently.
“Yes, to me. Why not? Don’t stir all the warmth out of your coffee; drink it. Though the letter might as well have been sent to you; it was nothing but Mrs. Pontellier from beginning to end.”
“Let me see it,” the young woman entreated.
“No; a letter concerns no one but the one who writes it and the one it’s written to.”
“Haven’t you just said it concerned me from beginning to end?”

“It was written about you, not to you. ‘Have you seen Mrs. Pontellier? How is she looking?’ he asks. ‘As Mrs. Pontellier says,’ or ‘as Mrs. Pontellier once said.’ ‘If Mrs. Pontellier should call upon you, play for her that Impromptu of Chopin’s, my favorite. I heard it here a day or two ago, but not as you play it. I should like to know how it affects her,’ and so on, as if he supposed we were constantly in each other’s society.”
“Let me see the letter.”
“Have you answered it?”
“Let me see the letter.”
“Then play the Impromptu for me.”
“It is growing late; what time do you have to be home?”
“Time doesn’t concern me. Your question seems a little rude. Play the Impromptu.”
“But you have told me nothing of yourself. What are you doing?”
“Painting!” laughed Edna. “I am becoming an artist. Think of it!”
“Ah! an artist! You have pretensions, Madame.”
“Why pretensions? Do you think I could not become an artist?”

“I do not know you well enough to say. I do not know your talent or your temperament. To be an artist includes much; one must possess many gifts—absolute gifts—which have not been acquired by one’s own effort. And, moreover, to succeed, the artist must possess the courageous soul.”
“What do you mean by the courageous soul?”
“Courageous, ma foi! The brave soul. The soul that dares and defies.”
“Show me the letter and play me the Impromptu. You see that I have persistence. Does that quality count for anything in art?”
“It counts with a foolish old woman whom you have captivated,” replied Mademoiselle, with her wriggling laugh.

The letter was right there in the drawer of the little table on which Edna had just set her coffee cup. Mademoiselle opened the drawer and drew out the topmost letter. She placed it in Edna’s hands, and without another word, went to the piano.

Mademoiselle played a soft interlude—an improvisation. She sat low at the instrument, and the lines of her body settled into ungraceful curves and angles that gave it an appearance of deformity. Gradually and imperceptibly the interlude melted into the soft opening minor chords of the Chopin Impromptu.

Edna did not know when the Impromptu began or ended. She sat in the corner of the sofa, reading Robert’s letter in the fading light. Mademoiselle had glided from the Chopin into the quivering love notes of Isolde’s song, and back again to the Impromptu with its soulful and poignant longing.

The shadows deepened in the little room. The music grew strange and fantastic—turbulent, insistent, plaintive and soft with entreaty. The shadows grew deeper. The music filled the room. It floated out upon the night, over the housetops, the crescent of the river, losing itself in the silence of the upper air.

Edna was sobbing, just as she had wept one midnight at Grand Isle when strange, new voices had awakened in her. She rose in some agitation to take her leave. “May I come again, Mademoiselle?” she asked from the threshold.
“Come whenever you feel like it. Be careful—the stairs and landings are dark; don’t stumble.”

Mademoiselle went back in and lit a candle. Robert’s letter was on the floor. She stooped and picked it up. It was crumpled and damp with tears. Mademoiselle smoothed it out, put it back in the envelope, and replaced it in the table drawer.

chapters.title: Chapter 22
paragraphs: One morning on his way into town, Mr. Pontellier stopped at the house of his old friend and family physician, Doctor Mandelet. The Doctor was a semi-retired physician, resting, as they say, on his laurels. He was known more for wisdom than for skill—leaving active practice to his assistants and younger contemporaries—and was much sought out for consultation. A few families he still attended out of friendship when they needed a doctor. The Pontelliers were among them.

Mr. Pontellier found the Doctor reading at his open study window. The house stood well back from the street, in the center of a lovely garden, so the old gentleman’s study was quiet and peaceful. He was an avid reader. He stared up with mild disapproval over his eyeglasses as Mr. Pontellier entered, wondering who had the nerve to disturb him at that hour.

“Ah, Pontellier! Not sick, I hope. Come and have a seat. What news do you bring this morning?” He was quite stout, with an abundance of gray hair and small blue eyes that age had robbed of much brightness but none of their sharpness.

“Oh! I’m never sick, Doctor. You know I come of tough fiber—from that old Creole stock of Pontelliers that dry up and finally blow away. I came to consult—no, not precisely to consult—to talk to you about Edna. I don’t know what ails her.”
“Madame Pontellier not well,” marveled the Doctor. “Why, I saw her—I think it was a week ago—walking along Canal Street, the picture of health, it seemed to me.”

“Yes, yes; she seems quite well,” said Mr. Pontellier, leaning forward and twirling his stick between his two hands; “but she doesn’t act well. She’s odd, she’s not like herself. I can’t make her out, and I thought perhaps you’d help me.”
“How does she act?” inquired the Doctor.
“Well, it isn’t easy to explain,” said Mr. Pontellier, throwing himself back in his chair. “She lets the housekeeping go to the dickens.”
“Well, well; women are not all alike, my dear Pontellier. We’ve got to consider—”

“I know that; I told you I couldn’t explain. Her whole attitude—toward me and everybody and everything—has changed. You know I have a quick temper, but I don’t want to quarrel or be rude to a woman, especially my wife; yet I’m driven to it, and feel like ten thousand devils after I’ve made a fool of myself. She’s making it devilishly uncomfortable for me,” he went on nervously. “She’s got some notion in her head about the eternal rights of women; and—you understand—we meet in the morning at the breakfast table.”
The old gentleman lifted his shaggy eyebrows, thrust out his lower lip, and tapped the arms of his chair with cushioned fingertips.
“What have you been doing to her, Pontellier?”
“Has she,” asked the Doctor, with a smile, “has she been associating of late with a circle of pseudo-intellectual women—super-spiritual superior beings? My wife has been telling me about them.”

“That’s the trouble,” broke in Mr. Pontellier, “she hasn’t been associating with anyone. She has abandoned her Tuesdays at home, dropped all her acquaintances, and goes tramping about by herself, moping on the streetcars, coming in after dark. I tell you she’s peculiar. I don’t like it; I feel a little worried about it.”
This was a new aspect for the Doctor. “Nothing hereditary?” he asked seriously. “Nothing peculiar about her family antecedents, is there?”

“Oh, no, indeed! She comes of sound old Presbyterian Kentucky stock. Her father, the Colonel, I’m told, used to atone for his weekday sins with his Sunday devotions. I know for a fact that his racehorses literally ran away with the prettiest bit of Kentucky farmland I ever laid eyes on. Margaret—you know Margaret—has all the Presbyterianism undiluted. And the youngest is something of a vixen. By the way, she gets married in a couple of weeks from now.”
“Send your wife up to the wedding,” exclaimed the Doctor, foreseeing a happy solution. “Let her stay among her own people for a while; it will do her good.”

“That’s what I want her to do. She won’t go to the wedding. She says a wedding is one of the most lamentable spectacles on earth. Fine thing for a woman to say to her husband!” exclaimed Mr. Pontellier, fuming at the recollection.

“Pontellier,” said the Doctor, after a moment’s reflection, “let your wife alone for a while. Don’t bother her, and don’t let her bother you. Woman, my dear friend, is a very peculiar and delicate organism—a sensitive and highly organized woman, such as I know Mrs. Pontellier to be, is especially peculiar. It would require an inspired psychologist to deal successfully with them. And when ordinary fellows like you and me attempt to cope with their idiosyncrasies the result is bungling. Most women are moody and whimsical. This is some passing whim of your wife, due to some cause which you and I needn’t try to fathom. But it will pass happily over, especially if you let her alone. Send her around to see me.”
“Oh! I couldn’t do that; there’d be no reason for it,” objected Mr. Pontellier.
“Then I’ll go around and see her,” said the Doctor. “I’ll drop in to dinner some evening en bon ami.”
“Do! By all means,” urged Mr. Pontellier. “What evening will you come? Say Thursday. Will you come Thursday?” he asked, rising to take his leave.
“Very well; Thursday. My wife may possibly have some engagement for me Thursday. If so, I shall let you know. Otherwise, you may expect me.”
Mr. Pontellier turned before leaving to say:

“I am going to New York on business very soon. I have a big scheme on hand, and want to be on the field proper to pull the ropes and handle the ribbons. We’ll let you in on the inside if you say so, Doctor,” he laughed.
“No, I thank you, my dear sir,” returned the Doctor. “I leave such ventures to you younger men with the fever of life still in your blood.”
“What I wanted to say,” continued Mr. Pontellier, with his hand on the knob; “I may have to be absent a good while. Would you advise me to take Edna along?”

“By all means, if she wishes to go. If not, leave her here. Don’t contradict her. The mood will pass, I assure you. It may take a month, two, three months—possibly longer, but it will pass; have patience.”
“Well, good-by, à jeudi,” said Mr. Pontellier, as he let himself out.
The Doctor would have liked during the course of the conversation to ask, “Is there any man in the case?”—but he knew his Creole too well to make such a blunder.
He did not resume his book immediately, but sat for a while meditatively looking out into the garden.

chapters.title: Chapter 23
paragraphs: Edna’s father was in the city and had been with them several days. She was not deeply or warmly attached to him, but they shared certain tastes, and in each other’s company they were companionable. His arrival came as a welcome disruption; it seemed to give her emotions a new direction.

He had come to buy a wedding gift for his daughter Janet and an outfit in which to make a respectable appearance at her wedding. Mr. Pontellier had chosen the bridal gift, as everyone immediately connected with him always deferred to his taste in such matters. And his suggestions on the question of dress—which too often assumes the nature of a problem—had been of inestimable value to his father-in-law. For the past few days, however, the old gentleman had been entirely in Edna’s hands, and in his company she was discovering a new set of sensations. He had been a colonel in the Confederate army and still maintained, along with the title, the military bearing that had always accompanied it. His hair and mustache were white and silky, emphasizing the rugged bronze of his face. He was tall and thin, and wore his coats padded, giving a fictitious breadth and depth to his shoulders and chest. Together Edna and her father made a distinguished pair and drew considerable notice during their walks. On his arrival she had begun by showing him her atelier and making a sketch of him. He took the whole matter very seriously. If her talent had been ten times greater than it was, it would not have surprised him, firmly convinced as he was that he had bequeathed to all his daughters the seeds of a masterful capability, which required only their own effort to be directed toward success.

Before her pencil he sat rigid and unyielding, as he had faced cannon fire in days gone by. He resented the intrusion of the children, who gaped at him with wide eyes from the doorway of their mother’s bright atelier. When they drew near, he waved them off with an expressive motion of his foot, unwilling to disturb the fixed lines of his face, his arms, his rigid shoulders.

Eager to entertain him, Edna invited Mademoiselle Reisz to come and meet him, promising him a treat in her piano-playing—but Mademoiselle declined. So instead they went together to a soirée musicale at the Ratignolles’. Monsieur and Madame Ratignolle made much of the Colonel, installing him as guest of honor and inviting him at once to dine with them the following Sunday, or any day he might choose. Madame coquetted with him in the most captivating and artless manner, with eyes and gestures and a profusion of compliments, until the Colonel’s old head felt thirty years younger on his padded shoulders. Edna marveled, uncomprehending. She herself was almost entirely without coquetry.

There were one or two men she noticed at the soirée, but she would never have felt moved to any kittenish display to attract their attention—no feline or feminine wiles to express herself toward them. Their personalities attracted her in a straightforward way. Her fancy selected them, and she was glad when a pause in the music gave them an opportunity to talk with her. Often on the street the glance of a stranger’s eyes had lingered in her memory, and sometimes had disturbed her.

Mr. Pontellier did not attend these soirées musicales. He found them bourgeois and preferred the diversions of the club. He had told Madame Ratignolle that the music at her evenings was too “heavy,” too far beyond his untrained comprehension. His excuse flattered her. But she disapproved of Mr. Pontellier’s club and was frank enough to say so to Edna.
“It’s a pity Mr. Pontellier doesn’t stay home more in the evenings. I think you would be more—well, if you don’t mind my saying it—more united, if he did.”
“Oh! dear no!” said Edna, with a blank look. “What should I do if he stayed home? We wouldn’t have anything to say to each other.”

She hadn’t much to say to her father either, for that matter—but he did not antagonize her. She found that he interested her, though she suspected it wouldn’t last long. For the first time in her life she felt as if she were truly getting to know him. He kept her busy attending to his wants. It amused her to do it. She would not allow a servant or one of the children to do for him anything she could do herself. Her husband noticed, and supposed it was the expression of a deep filial attachment he had never suspected.

The Colonel drank numerous “toddies” throughout the day, which left him, however, quite unperturbed. He was an expert at concocting strong drinks. He had even invented some, giving them fantastic names, and the preparation of these required various ingredients that fell to Edna to procure.

When Doctor Mandelet dined with the Pontelliers on Thursday he could discern in Mrs. Pontellier no trace of the morbid condition her husband had described. She was animated and in a manner radiant. She and her father had been to the racetrack, and their thoughts when they sat down to dinner were still occupied with the afternoon’s events, their talk still of the races. The Doctor had not kept up with racing. He had certain recollections of the sport from what he called “the good old times” when the Lecompte stables flourished, and he drew on this store of memories so as not to be left out or seem entirely devoid of the modern spirit. But he failed to impress the Colonel and was far from convincing him with his trumped-up knowledge of bygone days. Edna had staked her father on his last venture, with the most gratifying results for both of them. Besides, they had met some very charming people—Mrs. Mortimer Merriman and Mrs. James Highcamp, who were there with Alcée Arobin, had joined them and enlivened the hours in a way that warmed the Colonel to think of.

Mr. Pontellier had no particular leaning toward horseracing and was inclined to discourage it as a pastime, especially when he considered the fate of that bluegrass farm in Kentucky. He endeavored in a general way to express his disapproval and only succeeded in rousing the ire and opposition of his father-in-law. A spirited dispute followed, in which Edna warmly took her father’s side and the Doctor remained neutral.

He observed his hostess attentively from under his shaggy brows and noted a subtle change that had transformed her from the listless woman he had known into someone who seemed, for the moment, palpitant with the forces of life. Her speech was warm and energetic. There was no repression in her glance or gesture. She reminded him of some beautiful, sleek animal waking up in the sun.
The dinner was excellent. The claret was warm and the champagne cold, and under their beneficent influence the threatened unpleasantness melted and vanished with the fumes of the wine.
